morningSummary:
Good morning. RadiantWaves Media's Sunday edition begins with two urgent Nigerian stories: the Bayelsa boat disaster and a warning that armed groups in Zamfara have threatened to prevent voting in some communities. Governor Douye Diri says 23 bodies have been recovered and 24 survivors rescued after the boat carrying mourners capsized. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reports 24 deaths and 24 rescues. The figures differ across briefings and remain attributed. Preliminary findings point to overloading, no passenger manifest and the absence of life jackets. Police say the operator fled and the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. The governor has ordered a probe; the country needs transparent casualty reporting and enforceable waterway-safety rules.

Nigeria's electoral preparations face a second test. Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records were identified in the preliminary voters' register. INEC says its clean-up removed 1,609,553 invalid records, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states. These findings expose weaknesses that require an independent audit, but they do not prove a coordinated plan to rig the 2027 election. The commission must explain how the records entered the system, protect legitimate voters from wrongful exclusion and publish the results of its investigation. Separately, a SARI Global security report cited by PUNCH says bandit leaders in Anka, Zamfara, threatened to stop elections in their communities amid road blockades, attacks and displacement. The report's incident figures are private risk-intelligence estimates, not official government statistics.

Nigeria's opposition is also navigating a complicated legal and political landscape. Two separate court cases involving Atiku Abubakar and the ADC must not be confused: a 5 November judgment set aside the Mark-led ADC leadership process and Atiku's nomination, with the party saying it would appeal; a separate 20 November ruling refused to let Atiku and the ADC amend their Tinubu eligibility suit, leaving the original case pending and the allegation about the NYSC certificate undecided. The Coalition for Democracy has moved its summit to 30 November, with participating parties planning a one-day campaign pause. Opposition parties have alleged billboard destruction and restrictions on public venues; the state governments concerned deny political intimidation. The claims require evidence and impartial investigation. Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for an end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy, while Senate President Godswill Akpabio has urged parties to reject do-or-die politics.

On the economy, Nigeria's upstream regulator has opened bidding for 40 oil and gas blocks, with registration closing on 15 January 2027. The process could attract capital, but licences do not automatically translate into new production, jobs or public revenue. Ghana's proposed US$10 billion New Economy programme aims to boost agriculture, energy, technology, textiles and value-added minerals. A Global InfoAnalytics poll reported by Citi Newsroom says 51 per cent of young voters surveyed were satisfied with Ghana's 24-hour Economy policy, although the published summary does not provide full survey methodology. In South Africa, a broad coalition pact could sideline the DA in three Gauteng metros even though it was the largest single party in each; final positions and governing arrangements remain outstanding.

Europe faces pressure over living costs, industrial jobs and public services. France's sixth weekend of demonstrations drew lower turnout, with the Interior Ministry counting 82,500 people and organisers estimating 150,000. In Lisbon, thousands marched over wages, rents and affordability; Reuters cited Eurostat data showing average Portuguese earnings in 2025 were 37 per cent below the EU average. Germany's IG Metall union says 23,000 workers across 19 companies will strike on Monday, 23 November, in a dispute over pay and secure jobs. Belgium's air-traffic controller Skeyes says it cannot guarantee regular services from 7am to 9pm on Monday, and airports expect most flights to be cancelled. The UK and EU have agreed a cooperation package on food trade, carbon markets and youth opportunities, but the detailed rules remain to be implemented. Ukraine and Britain have agreed to manufacture Ukrainian-designed strike drones in the UK.

In the United Kingdom, October government borrowing came in at £17 billion, below the £18 billion forecast, and earlier borrowing was revised down. Yet the debt-interest bill reached a record £11.2 billion for October, showing that public finances remain under strain. In the United States, President Donald Trump's new executive order requires federal contractors to coordinate with the White House before responding to certain congressional inquiries. Democrats call it an attack on oversight; the administration says it is protecting executive privilege. The legal boundary remains contested. In Canada, Defence Minister David McGuinty says military cooperation with Washington continues despite reports of a classified Pentagon memo; the document has not been made public and its exact scope remains unclear.

Asia's headlines include a deadly Indonesian factory fire, the resignation of South Korea's education minister after an AI-assisted cheating scandal, a US–China dispute over Chinese telecom firms' direct access to American phone numbers and a new disagreement between Myanmar's military-backed government and ASEAN over political representation. Australia and China have agreed to establish a dialogue on AI safety and governance while continuing to manage wider trade and security differences.

The Middle East remains tense. Bahrain says an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility and that its air defences intercepted further attacks; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to have targeted US positions, a claim not independently confirmed by US Central Command. UKMTO reported two tanker incidents near Oman's Khasab, but responsibility remains unclear and Iran's separate mine claim has not been linked independently to either report. In Iraq, a fire involving a gas pipeline at the Hartha power station killed at least four people and injured 35. UNIFIL has begun handing over some southern Lebanon positions to the Lebanese army ahead of the peacekeeping mission's mandate ending on 31 December 2026.

At COP31 in Türkiye, negotiators presented a revised climate package intended to secure consensus on fossil-fuel language and adaptation finance. A formal final decision was not confirmed in the sources reviewed at 07:28 CET. Global technology shares have also suffered a sharp repricing: Reuters says the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3 per cent on Friday and 10 per cent over the week as investors reassessed AI valuations and spending. In sport, Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix, while Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev are scheduled to contest the ATP Finals title in Turin.

featured.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: death toll rises as governor orders investigation and safety enforcement
featured.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
featured.summary: Governor Douye Diri says 23 bodies have been recovered and 24 survivors rescued; AP, citing NEMA, reports 24 deaths. The discrepancy remains unresolved as authorities investigate overloading, missing passenger records and the absence of life jackets.
featured.content:
A boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. Preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets.

The casualty figures are not yet consistent across reports. PUNCH carried the governor's update of 23 recovered bodies and 24 survivors. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reported at least 24 deaths and 24 rescues. The earlier police account had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving reports from separate briefings; RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than presenting one figure as final. Police said the boat reportedly developed a mechanical fault, that passengers urged the operator to head for the riverbank, and that the operator allegedly continued before the vessel capsized. The operator reportedly fled, while the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. Those claims require investigation and do not establish criminal guilt.

President Bola Tinubu expressed condolences and directed federal disaster-response agencies to support recovery and rescue work. PUNCH reported that he observed a minute of silence at the Ibadan APC rally and said Vice-President Kashim Shettima would visit Bayelsa. The governor has also announced plans for modern boats and a Maritime Task Force. Those proposals must be matched by transparent budgets, inspection schedules, passenger manifests, enforceable capacity limits, compulsory life jackets, trained operators and reliable rescue capacity.

The investigation should establish how many people were on board, whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and which agencies were responsible for enforcement. Replacing unsafe boats alone will not solve a system in which overloading and weak inspections can become normal practice. Families need an accurate casualty list, a transparent investigation and practical safeguards before the next journey.

topStories.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: NEMA confirms 24 deaths as rescue operation continues
topStories.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
topStories.summary: Reuters reported on Sunday that NEMA confirmed 24 deaths and 24 survivors after Friday's boat disaster. This updates earlier public figures of 23 bodies recovered by Governor Douye Diri; authorities have not published a final passenger manifest or complete account of everyone aboard.
topStories.content:
Reuters reported on 22 November that at least 24 people died when a crowded boat carrying mourners to a funeral in Bayelsa State capsized on Friday, 20 November. The National Emergency Management Agency said 24 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The report brings the national agency's figure into line with the 24 deaths cited by the Associated Press. It is a further update to the governor's earlier statement, carried by PUNCH late on Saturday, that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued.

The vessel was travelling from Ayama to Ukubie in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area for a burial ceremony. Police initially reported a mechanical fault. The governor said preliminary findings pointed to overloading, the absence of a passenger manifest and passengers not wearing life jackets. Police accounts reported by AP say passengers allegedly asked the operator to steer towards shore after the problem developed; the operator reportedly fled and the boat manager was taken into custody. These are investigative accounts, not findings of guilt.

The state government has announced an investigation and plans for a Maritime Task Force and modern boats. The central questions remain: how many people boarded, whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, whether life jackets were available, who was responsible for inspection and why safety rules were not enforced. A final casualty list and transparent findings are essential for affected families and public accountability.

topStories.title: Zamfara bandits threaten to block 2027 voting as road control deepens
topStories.summary: A SARI Global security report cited by Sunday PUNCH says armed leaders warned community representatives in Anka that elections would not be allowed. The report also describes road blockades, attacks, levies and displacement; its figures are not official government statistics.
topStories.content:
Sunday PUNCH reported on 22 November that a SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026 described a threat by bandit leaders in Anka Local Government Area, Zamfara State, to prevent elections in their communities. The report says armed groups have tightened control over roads, burned vehicles, imposed a ₦50 million levy on communities in Dansadau District and displaced more than 300 residents.

According to SARI Global, Zamfara recorded 69 security incidents and 137 fatalities in October, making it the country's most incident-dense state in the firm's assessment. The report also says abduction cases nationwide rose to 55 in October from 27 in September. It describes attacks on roads, vehicles and escorted convoys, including an ambush in which at least 20 people were reportedly killed. These are figures and assessments from the private risk-intelligence report as reported by PUNCH, not a consolidated official national security dataset.

The alleged election threat is especially serious because it suggests armed groups may seek to control not only movement and commerce but also political participation. Zamfara has 14 local government areas and 3,529 polling units, according to INEC figures cited by PUNCH. If communities cannot travel safely, campaign, register or reach polling units, formal election dates alone will not guarantee equal participation.

Security agencies and INEC need to explain how they will protect roads, communities, election staff, observers and voters without placing civilians at greater risk. The government should publish credible incident data and the outcomes of operations, while avoiding claims that a threat has been neutralised before residents can safely resume normal movement.

topStories.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026; INEC figures as reported by PUNCH
topStories.whyItMatters: An election cannot be considered inclusive if armed groups can prevent entire communities from voting or moving freely.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Track security deployments, road access, displacement, investigations into attacks and INEC's contingency plans for affected polling units.

topStories.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
topStories.summary: Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records entered the preliminary register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid records, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states; the findings do not prove a coordinated rigging plot.
topStories.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says questionable records were flagged during the nationwide display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and that INEC later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, told the newspaper that some registration officers had used their official login details to introduce questionable records but could not explain their actions.

INEC's wider clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 records: 1,608,660 confirmed invalid registrations and 873 records belonging to verified deceased people. The commission also identified 54 people across 10 states as implicated in registration irregularities. The figures are attributed to INEC statements reported by PUNCH; the commission's final register and any resulting disciplinary or criminal proceedings remain important next steps.

The concern is not limited to photographs. A credible register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Yiaga Africa's Samson Itodo and other civil-society representatives told Sunday PUNCH that the register is foundational to electoral credibility and called for an independent forensic audit with safeguards for personal data. The European Union Election Observation Mission had already identified weaknesses in Nigeria's register after the 2023 election, including deceased, emigrated and internally migrated voters and acknowledged under-age registrations.

The discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. One civil-society representative quoted by PUNCH explicitly warned against that conclusion without concrete evidence, while saying the irregularities could be exploited if left unresolved. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate and prosecute anyone found guilty. The commission should publish how the controls failed, the audit trail, the affected record categories and a clear process for eligible voters to challenge errors before the final register is released.

topStories.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements; comments by Yiaga Africa and other civil-society representatives reported by PUNCH
topStories.whyItMatters: A trustworthy register is the foundation of a credible election. Weak controls can undermine confidence before polling day, while careless clean-up can wrongly exclude eligible citizens.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, the final register, publication of audit findings, any prosecutions and accessible procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.
topStories.label: INEC / VOTER REGISTER

topStories.title: Separate court cases leave Atiku and the ADC facing two different legal tests
topStories.summary: A 5 November Federal High Court judgment set aside the Mark-led ADC leadership process and Atiku Abubakar's nomination; the ADC said it would appeal. Separately, on 20 November, a judge refused to let Atiku and the ADC amend their Tinubu eligibility suit, leaving the original case pending.
topStories.content:
Two separate legal proceedings are shaping the ADC's position ahead of Nigeria's 2027 election, and they must not be reported as one case. On 5 November, the Federal High Court in Abuja, presided over by Justice Peter Lifu, nullified the David Mark-led ADC leadership structure and set aside decisions taken under it, including the party process that produced Atiku Abubakar as its presidential candidate. The challenge was brought by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe, who argued that the leadership had not emerged through a valid national convention. Reuters reported that the ADC rejected the judgment as politically motivated and said it would appeal.

In a separate pre-election suit filed by Atiku and the ADC against President Bola Tinubu, the APC and INEC, Justice Inyang Ekwo on 20 November refused the plaintiffs permission to amend their case. The proposed amendments were rejected on procedural grounds because they would introduce new facts outside the constitutional 14-day period for pre-election matters. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. The case concerns allegations about an NYSC discharge certificate submitted in support of Tinubu's nomination; Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate. The ruling did not determine whether the certificate is genuine and did not dismiss the substantive suit.

The national ADC leadership judgment and the Tinubu eligibility case therefore have different parties, legal questions and procedural positions. PUNCH reported that INEC had received notice of the appeal against the 5 November judgment and would await the Court of Appeal's decision. The reports reviewed for this edition do not establish that the appeal has been finally decided or that the trial judgment has been set aside.

The public interest is the rule of law: court orders must be respected, appeals must be heard fairly, and political allegations must be tested through evidence. Neither the ADC's claim of political motivation nor the allegation about Tinubu's certificate should be presented as a judicial finding unless a court has actually made that finding.

topStories.source: Reuters, 5 November 2026; PUNCH, 5 and 20 November 2026; Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; INEC comments reported by PUNCH
topStories.whyItMatters: The cases affect opposition candidate selection and presidential eligibility, but conflating them can mislead voters about what the courts have actually decided.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Track the Court of Appeal proceedings in the ADC leadership case and the next substantive hearing in the separate Tinubu eligibility suit.
topStories.label: ADC / TWO DISTINCT COURT CASES

topStories.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
topStories.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.
topStories.content:
Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. Sunday PUNCH reports that the ADC and other opposition groups alleged that their campaign materials were being removed and that access to public facilities was being restricted.

In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

topStories.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda
topStories.summary: At Saturday's Mapo Hall rally, President Bola Tinubu urged supporters to stay the course, highlighted the proposed Yutong–Leyland factory reopening and made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark interpreted by some outlets as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM.
topStories.content:
President Bola Tinubu used his visit to Ibadan on Saturday to seek South-West support for his administration and the APC's 2027 campaign. The Guardian reported that he told traditional rulers, led by the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, that the sacrifices associated with his economic reforms would lead to greater prosperity. Tinubu cited an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the former Leyland Automobile Assembly Plant, saying the project could support vehicle assembly and employment.

At the Mapo Hall rally, he endorsed APC candidates for Oyo, Ogun and Lagos and made a remark about a group he called the 'palẹmọ' faction. Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. RadiantWaves distinguishes the President's words from media interpretation.

The political test for the administration is whether the promised industrial activity, employment and economic reforms produce measurable benefits for households and businesses. The opposition is entitled to challenge the record, while the government should publish project milestones, financing details, job estimates and delivery dates.

topStories.title: Nigeria opens bidding portal for 40 oil and gas blocks
topStories.summary: The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission says registration opened on 20 November and closes on 15 January 2027. The offer includes 17 onshore, 14 shallow-water and nine deep-offshore blocks.
topStories.content:
The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission has opened the portal for its 2026 oil and gas licensing round, offering 40 blocks to prospective investors. PUNCH reported on 22 November that registration began on Friday, 20 November, and will close on 15 January 2027. The blocks comprise 17 onshore, 14 shallow-water and nine deep-offshore assets.

The regulator says the process will run through five stages: registration and prequalification, access to data, submission of technical and commercial bids, technical evaluation and a commercial conference. A pre-bid conference is scheduled for Lagos on 16 December 2026. The commission says the portal provides the list of blocks, bidding guidance and frequently asked questions.

The licensing round is part of Nigeria's effort to attract capital, increase upstream production and improve competitiveness in the global energy market. However, a licensing round is not the same as immediate new production or revenue. Exploration, financing, environmental approvals, infrastructure, security and commercial development can take years. The credibility of the process will depend on transparent bid evaluation, clear contract terms, environmental safeguards, host-community engagement and public reporting of awards and obligations.

topStories.title: France sees sixth weekend of protests over living costs, public services and student conditions
topStories.summary: Reuters reports that turnout fell at largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday: the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 nationwide, while organisers estimated 150,000. Cost-of-living and student-rights concerns remain.
topStories.content:
France experienced a sixth consecutive weekend of demonstrations on Saturday, 21 November, over the cost of living, student rights and public services. Reuters reported that the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 participants nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris. Organisers estimated 150,000 nationwide, including 45,000 in the capital. Both figures are attributed estimates and should not be combined. The previous Saturday's Interior Ministry count was 106,000, while organisers had estimated 200,000.

The movement began in September with students demanding renovated school buildings, more teachers and university reforms. It broadened into a wider campaign over purchasing power, public services and policing, drawing in trade unions and political activists. Reuters reported that about 70,000 security personnel were deployed and that most demonstrations were peaceful, although sporadic violence was reported, including in Marseille.

The lower turnout offers the government some respite, but does not establish that the underlying grievances have been resolved. Housing costs, wages, education resources and trust in policing remain politically sensitive as France approaches the 2027 presidential contest. The demonstrations should be assessed by their demands and the government's response, not simply by crowd size.

topStories.whyItMatters: The demonstrations connect everyday affordability, education and public-service quality with questions of policing and democratic accountability.

topStories.title: Belgium warns of major flight cancellations during Monday's national strike
topStories.summary: Air traffic controller Skeyes says it cannot guarantee regular air traffic from 7am to 9pm on Monday, 23 November. Brussels Airport expects most flights to be cancelled; essential emergency flights may continue.
topStories.content:
Belgium is preparing for major disruption to air travel on Monday, 23 November, after air traffic controller Skeyes said staffing levels would not allow it to guarantee the safe handling of regular air traffic between 7am and 9pm. AFP reported that Brussels Airport expects the majority of arriving and departing flights to be cancelled. Charleroi Airport said the strike would shut down regular operations across the country's airports for the day.

The action is part of a national strike against government austerity measures and proposed savings intended to reduce Belgium's budget deficit. Skeyes said essential minimum services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would remain available. Passengers should check directly with their airline and airport before travelling, because schedules and cancellation policies may change.

The dispute reflects broader tensions over public spending, government cost-cutting and the effect of austerity on workers and essential services.

topStories.title: Trump order puts federal contractors at centre of coming congressional oversight battle
topStories.summary: An executive order requires federal contractors to consult the White House and agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries and to withhold material the administration considers privileged. Democrats call it an attack on oversight; the White House says it protects executive privilege.
topStories.content:
President Donald Trump issued an executive order late on Friday requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with the administration before responding to certain inquiries from Congress. The Associated Press reported that companies must coordinate with the White House and relevant agencies on responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. Contractors that do not comply could face termination of their contracts or suspension from future federal work.

The order applies to a large network of companies that do business with the federal government. It comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January and have signalled investigations into government contracts, including payments to companies linked to the President's family. The White House has also instructed agencies to seek approval before agreeing to congressional testimony.

Democratic lawmakers described the order as an attack on Congress's constitutional oversight authority and argued that contractors have a duty to provide truthful information when lawfully requested. The White House says it is protecting executive privilege from congressional overreach. Presidents of both parties have asserted executive privilege, but its scope is limited and disputes can lead to prolonged legal battles. Whether communications held by outside contractors qualify for the protection may be tested in court.

The central question is how to protect legitimate confidential executive deliberations without preventing Congress from investigating public spending, conflicts of interest or possible wrongdoing. The order does not settle that constitutional dispute; it creates a new point of conflict between the executive branch and the incoming Congress.

topStories.summary: An AP report says three people died and 36 workers remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy factory in Banten. Fifteen people were rescued, including four injured; the cause has not been established.
topStories.content:
A fire swept through the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Serang district, Banten province, on Saturday, 21 November. The Associated Press reported that three people had died and 36 workers remained unaccounted for as rescue teams searched the damaged facility. Fifteen people were rescued alive, including four injured workers. The factory produces Milkita milk-based sweets and snacks.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said search operations were continuing. More than 12 hours after the fire began, flames were still burning in parts of the facility, according to local rescue officials. Survivors suggested that the blaze may have started in a cooling unit on the third floor, but officials had not established the cause and had not confirmed whether all missing workers were inside when the fire began.

The immediate priority is locating missing workers and identifying the dead and injured. A later investigation will need to establish how the fire started, whether alarms and emergency exits were adequate, how quickly workers were evacuated and whether workplace fire-safety standards were followed. The incident adds to wider concerns about industrial safety and emergency preparedness.

worldNews.title: Trump order puts federal contractors at centre of coming congressional oversight battle
worldNews.summary: An executive order requires federal contractors to consult the White House and agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries and to withhold material the administration considers privileged. Democrats call it an attack on oversight; the White House says it protects executive privilege.
worldNews.content:
President Donald Trump issued an executive order late on Friday requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with the administration before responding to certain inquiries from Congress. The Associated Press reported that companies must coordinate with the White House and relevant agencies on responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. Contractors that do not comply could face termination of their contracts or suspension from future federal work.

The order applies to a large network of companies that do business with the federal government. It comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January and have signalled investigations into government contracts, including payments to companies linked to the President's family. The White House has also instructed agencies to seek approval before agreeing to congressional testimony.

Democratic lawmakers described the order as an attack on Congress's constitutional oversight authority and argued that contractors have a duty to provide truthful information when lawfully requested. The White House says it is protecting executive privilege from congressional overreach. Presidents of both parties have asserted executive privilege, but its scope is limited and disputes can lead to prolonged legal battles. Whether communications held by outside contractors qualify for the protection may be tested in court.

The central question is how to protect legitimate confidential executive deliberations without preventing Congress from investigating public spending, conflicts of interest or possible wrongdoing. The order does not settle that constitutional dispute; it creates a new point of conflict between the executive branch and the incoming Congress.

worldNews.content:
Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said on 21 November that he had seen no change in military cooperation with the United States, despite a Washington Post report about a classified Pentagon directive imposing new restrictions on defence ties. Speaking to Reuters at a security conference in Halifax, McGuinty said the two militaries continued to work closely on continental defence, counter-narcotics operations, integrated missile systems and responses to threats in North American airspace.

The Washington Post report cited officials familiar with the memo but said it had not seen the document. Reuters reported that the Pentagon had not responded to its request for comment; a Pentagon spokesperson was quoted elsewhere as saying the guidance did not affect NATO, NORAD or intelligence operations. Republican Senator Mike Rounds said the memo contained no major measures beyond longstanding practice. The document's exact scope and practical effect therefore remain unclear.

McGuinty said Canada's 70-year NORAD relationship with the United States remained effective, while arguing that Canada must assume more responsibility for its own defence, particularly in the Arctic. Canada says it reached NATO's 2 per cent GDP spending target in 2025 and plans to increase defence spending to 5 per cent by 2035. The episode illustrates the tension between maintaining an integrated continental defence system and reducing strategic dependence on a neighbour whose political rhetoric has unsettled Canadian leaders.

worldNews.content:
A Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, caught fire after being struck by two drones in international waters west of Russia's Gogland island on Saturday, 21 November, and later drifted into Finnish waters. Reuters reported that all 16 crew members evacuated into lifeboats and were transferred to another Russian vessel. Finnish authorities were leading the rescue effort while the fire continued.

The vessel is owned by Oboronlogistika, a company that provides logistics services to Russia's Defence Ministry and is under US sanctions. Finnish officials said its cargo had not been confirmed, although it could include military materiel.

The incident has created a maritime and security challenge for Finland and other Baltic states. Finnish authorities imposed temporary aviation and maritime restrictions, and Sweden and Estonia assisted with security and rescue operations. Finnish officials also said a Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly entering Finnish airspace during the response. These details do not establish a deliberate attack on Finland or confirm the cargo carried by the ship.

The episode illustrates how the war in Ukraine can create risks beyond the battlefield, particularly when military-linked shipping, drones and rescue operations intersect near NATO territory.

worldNews.category: Middle East / Lebanon / United Nations / Security
worldNews.summary: UNIFIL's mission chief says some positions are being transferred to the Lebanese army as the force prepares for its mandate to end on 31 December 2026. The UN Security Council has authorised a phased drawdown and withdrawal during 2027.
worldNews.content:
UNIFIL has begun handing over some of its positions in southern Lebanon to the Lebanese army, mission chief Diodato Abagnara said on Saturday, according to Lebanon's National News Agency as reported by Anadolu. He warned against a security vacuum after the peacekeeping mission ends and said monitoring and reporting violations, humanitarian assistance and civilian protection remain important.

The UN Security Council's Resolution 2790 (2025) extended UNIFIL's mandate for a final time until 31 December 2026 and directed an orderly drawdown and withdrawal beginning at the end of the year, to be completed within one year. The resolution calls for stronger Lebanese army deployment and international support for its capabilities. UNIFIL has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978, with its mandate expanded after the 2006 conflict.

The handover is not simply an administrative transfer. Southern Lebanon remains affected by conflict and violations of the cessation-of-hostilities arrangement. The transition will depend on the Lebanese state's ability to provide security, the support available to its armed forces and whether a replacement international monitoring arrangement is agreed.

worldNews.category: Asia / Myanmar / ASEAN / Diplomacy / Human Rights
worldNews.summary: Myanmar's foreign ministry says ASEAN's refusal to grant full political representation is unfair. ASEAN leaders say representation could be restored gradually if the authorities make progress on the bloc's five-point peace consensus.
worldNews.content:
Myanmar's military-backed government criticised an ASEAN decision as unfair and imbalanced on Saturday, 21 November, accusing the regional grouping of discriminatory treatment because Myanmar is not granted full representation at its summits. Reuters reported that the foreign ministry said the decision issued at the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila failed to reflect what the authorities described as positive measures taken by the government.

ASEAN leaders said at the summit that full political representation could be restored gradually if Myanmar made progress on the bloc's five-point consensus, a framework intended to end the post-coup crisis. The Myanmar statement said there were no political prisoners and that more than 126,000 prisoners had received pardons or amnesties since the coup. The United Nations and human-rights organisations have reported thousands of political prisoners, so the government's claim is disputed and should not be presented as an established fact.

Myanmar has remained in turmoil since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021, triggering a civil war. Reuters cited UN estimates of about 100,000 deaths and more than 3.5 million people displaced. The ASEAN position reflects continued pressure for an end to violence and meaningful dialogue, while the authorities in Naypyidaw are seeking greater regional legitimacy.

The dispute is not simply about protocol at summits. It concerns whether regional engagement can encourage a political settlement, protect civilians and create conditions for a return to inclusive government.

electionWatch.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
electionWatch.summary: Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records entered the preliminary register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid records, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states; the findings do not prove a coordinated rigging plot.
electionWatch.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says questionable records were flagged during the nationwide display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and that INEC later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, told the newspaper that some registration officers had used their official login details to introduce questionable records but could not explain their actions.

INEC's wider clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 records: 1,608,660 confirmed invalid registrations and 873 records belonging to verified deceased people. The commission also identified 54 people across 10 states as implicated in registration irregularities. The figures are attributed to INEC statements reported by PUNCH; the commission's final register and any resulting disciplinary or criminal proceedings remain important next steps.

The concern is not limited to photographs. A credible register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Yiaga Africa's Samson Itodo and other civil-society representatives told Sunday PUNCH that the register is foundational to electoral credibility and called for an independent forensic audit with safeguards for personal data. The European Union Election Observation Mission had already identified weaknesses in Nigeria's register after the 2023 election, including deceased, emigrated and internally migrated voters and acknowledged under-age registrations.

The discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. One civil-society representative quoted by PUNCH explicitly warned against that conclusion without concrete evidence, while saying the irregularities could be exploited if left unresolved. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate and prosecute anyone found guilty. The commission should publish how the controls failed, the audit trail, the affected record categories and a clear process for eligible voters to challenge errors before the final register is released.

electionWatch.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements; comments by Yiaga Africa and other civil-society representatives reported by PUNCH
electionWatch.whyItMatters: A trustworthy register is the foundation of a credible election. Weak controls can undermine confidence before polling day, while careless clean-up can wrongly exclude eligible citizens.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, the final register, publication of audit findings, any prosecutions and accessible procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.

electionWatch.title: Separate court cases leave Atiku and the ADC facing two different legal tests
electionWatch.summary: A 5 November Federal High Court judgment set aside the Mark-led ADC leadership process and Atiku Abubakar's nomination; the ADC said it would appeal. Separately, on 20 November, a judge refused to let Atiku and the ADC amend their Tinubu eligibility suit, leaving the original case pending.
electionWatch.content:
Two separate legal proceedings are shaping the ADC's position ahead of Nigeria's 2027 election, and they must not be reported as one case. On 5 November, the Federal High Court in Abuja, presided over by Justice Peter Lifu, nullified the David Mark-led ADC leadership structure and set aside decisions taken under it, including the party process that produced Atiku Abubakar as its presidential candidate. The challenge was brought by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe, who argued that the leadership had not emerged through a valid national convention. Reuters reported that the ADC rejected the judgment as politically motivated and said it would appeal.

In a separate pre-election suit filed by Atiku and the ADC against President Bola Tinubu, the APC and INEC, Justice Inyang Ekwo on 20 November refused the plaintiffs permission to amend their case. The proposed amendments were rejected on procedural grounds because they would introduce new facts outside the constitutional 14-day period for pre-election matters. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. The case concerns allegations about an NYSC discharge certificate submitted in support of Tinubu's nomination; Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate. The ruling did not determine whether the certificate is genuine and did not dismiss the substantive suit.

The national ADC leadership judgment and the Tinubu eligibility case therefore have different parties, legal questions and procedural positions. PUNCH reported that INEC had received notice of the appeal against the 5 November judgment and would await the Court of Appeal's decision. The reports reviewed for this edition do not establish that the appeal has been finally decided or that the trial judgment has been set aside.

The public interest is the rule of law: court orders must be respected, appeals must be heard fairly, and political allegations must be tested through evidence. Neither the ADC's claim of political motivation nor the allegation about Tinubu's certificate should be presented as a judicial finding unless a court has actually made that finding.

electionWatch.source: Reuters, 5 November 2026; PUNCH, 5 and 20 November 2026; Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; INEC comments reported by PUNCH
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The cases affect opposition candidate selection and presidential eligibility, but conflating them can mislead voters about what the courts have actually decided.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Track the Court of Appeal proceedings in the ADC leadership case and the next substantive hearing in the separate Tinubu eligibility suit.
electionWatch.label: ADC / TWO DISTINCT COURT CASES

electionWatch.title: Opposition coalition moves summit to 30 November and plans a one-day campaign pause
electionWatch.summary: The Coalition for Democracy says ADC, APM, NDC, a PDP faction, PRP and SDP members will pause campaigns nationwide on 30 November to attend a summit. The meeting is intended to produce a common agreement, not yet a single presidential ticket.
electionWatch.content:
The Coalition for Democracy has rescheduled its second summit from Monday, 23 November, to Monday, 30 November 2026, after member parties said campaign schedules could prevent presidential candidates, national chairmen and other leaders from attending. The committee's statement, signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman, says participating parties will pause campaign activities nationwide for the day so their representatives can attend.

The coalition emerged from the G100 Opposition Summit held in Abuja on 31 August. Its participating platforms include the African Democratic Congress, Allied Peoples Movement, Nigeria Democratic Congress, a faction of the Peoples Democratic Party, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party. Organisers say the 30 November meeting is intended to finalise and sign a common agreement ahead of the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

The move is evidence of coordination, but it is not proof that the parties have selected one presidential candidate or resolved their internal disputes. The coalition's credibility will depend on transparent decision-making, a clear policy programme, a fair process for any joint candidacy and respect for each party's constitutional procedures. Voters should be able to distinguish a temporary political agreement from a formal merger or a settled ticket.

electionWatch.title: Zamfara bandits threaten to block 2027 voting as road control deepens
electionWatch.summary: A SARI Global security report cited by Sunday PUNCH says armed leaders warned community representatives in Anka that elections would not be allowed. The report also describes road blockades, attacks, levies and displacement; its figures are not official government statistics.
electionWatch.content:
Sunday PUNCH reported on 22 November that a SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026 described a threat by bandit leaders in Anka Local Government Area, Zamfara State, to prevent elections in their communities. The report says armed groups have tightened control over roads, burned vehicles, imposed a ₦50 million levy on communities in Dansadau District and displaced more than 300 residents.

According to SARI Global, Zamfara recorded 69 security incidents and 137 fatalities in October, making it the country's most incident-dense state in the firm's assessment. The report also says abduction cases nationwide rose to 55 in October from 27 in September. It describes attacks on roads, vehicles and escorted convoys, including an ambush in which at least 20 people were reportedly killed. These are figures and assessments from the private risk-intelligence report as reported by PUNCH, not a consolidated official national security dataset.

The alleged election threat is especially serious because it suggests armed groups may seek to control not only movement and commerce but also political participation. Zamfara has 14 local government areas and 3,529 polling units, according to INEC figures cited by PUNCH. If communities cannot travel safely, campaign, register or reach polling units, formal election dates alone will not guarantee equal participation.

Security agencies and INEC need to explain how they will protect roads, communities, election staff, observers and voters without placing civilians at greater risk. The government should publish credible incident data and the outcomes of operations, while avoiding claims that a threat has been neutralised before residents can safely resume normal movement.

electionWatch.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026; INEC figures as reported by PUNCH
electionWatch.whyItMatters: An election cannot be considered inclusive if armed groups can prevent entire communities from voting or moving freely.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Track security deployments, road access, displacement, investigations into attacks and INEC's contingency plans for affected polling units.
electionWatch.label: ZAMFARA / ELECTION SECURITY

electionWatch.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
electionWatch.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.
electionWatch.content:
Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. Sunday PUNCH reports that the ADC and other opposition groups alleged that their campaign materials were being removed and that access to public facilities was being restricted.

In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

electionWatch.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; statements by ADC representatives and Benue State Government
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Political competition is not fair if parties cannot campaign peacefully and lawfully. Allegations of intimidation require evidence and a response from the authorities concerned.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Seek police records, local government venue policies, documented complaints and outcomes of any investigations into billboard destruction.

electionWatch.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda
electionWatch.summary: At Saturday's Mapo Hall rally, President Bola Tinubu urged supporters to stay the course, highlighted the proposed Yutong–Leyland factory reopening and made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark interpreted by some outlets as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM.
electionWatch.content:
President Bola Tinubu used his visit to Ibadan on Saturday to seek South-West support for his administration and the APC's 2027 campaign. The Guardian reported that he told traditional rulers, led by the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, that the sacrifices associated with his economic reforms would lead to greater prosperity. Tinubu cited an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the former Leyland Automobile Assembly Plant, saying the project could support vehicle assembly and employment.

At the Mapo Hall rally, he endorsed APC candidates for Oyo, Ogun and Lagos and made a remark about a group he called the 'palẹmọ' faction. Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. RadiantWaves distinguishes the President's words from media interpretation.

The political test for the administration is whether the promised industrial activity, employment and economic reforms produce measurable benefits for households and businesses. The opposition is entitled to challenge the record, while the government should publish project milestones, financing details, job estimates and delivery dates.

electionWatch.imageNote: Existing repository image used only as an illustrative portrait, not an event photograph.
electionWatch.source: The Guardian Nigeria, 22 November 2026; Naija News, 22 November 2026; Channels Television, 21 November 2026
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Political rallies are part of democratic campaigning, but policy claims should be assessed against delivery, measurable outcomes and public accountability.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for details of the Yutong–Leyland agreement, project timetable, financing, employment commitments and responses from the Oyo State Government and opposition parties.

articles.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: death toll rises as governor orders investigation and safety enforcement
articles.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
articles.summary: Governor Douye Diri says 23 bodies have been recovered and 24 survivors rescued; AP, citing NEMA, reports 24 deaths. The discrepancy remains unresolved as authorities investigate overloading, missing passenger records and the absence of life jackets.
articles.content:
A boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. Preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets.

The casualty figures are not yet consistent across reports. PUNCH carried the governor's update of 23 recovered bodies and 24 survivors. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reported at least 24 deaths and 24 rescues. The earlier police account had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving reports from separate briefings; RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than presenting one figure as final. Police said the boat reportedly developed a mechanical fault, that passengers urged the operator to head for the riverbank, and that the operator allegedly continued before the vessel capsized. The operator reportedly fled, while the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. Those claims require investigation and do not establish criminal guilt.

President Bola Tinubu expressed condolences and directed federal disaster-response agencies to support recovery and rescue work. PUNCH reported that he observed a minute of silence at the Ibadan APC rally and said Vice-President Kashim Shettima would visit Bayelsa. The governor has also announced plans for modern boats and a Maritime Task Force. Those proposals must be matched by transparent budgets, inspection schedules, passenger manifests, enforceable capacity limits, compulsory life jackets, trained operators and reliable rescue capacity.

The investigation should establish how many people were on board, whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and which agencies were responsible for enforcement. Replacing unsafe boats alone will not solve a system in which overloading and weak inspections can become normal practice. Families need an accurate casualty list, a transparent investigation and practical safeguards before the next journey.

articles.whyItMatters: Waterway safety is a public responsibility. A manifest, safe passenger capacity, life jackets and effective enforcement can prevent a routine journey from becoming a mass-casualty event.
articles.whatHappensNext: Track the official casualty reconciliation, investigation findings, any charges, the status of the boat manager, the promised Maritime Task Force and procurement of safer vessels.

articles.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
articles.summary: Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records entered the preliminary register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid records, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states; the findings do not prove a coordinated rigging plot.
articles.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says questionable records were flagged during the nationwide display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and that INEC later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, told the newspaper that some registration officers had used their official login details to introduce questionable records but could not explain their actions.

INEC's wider clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 records: 1,608,660 confirmed invalid registrations and 873 records belonging to verified deceased people. The commission also identified 54 people across 10 states as implicated in registration irregularities. The figures are attributed to INEC statements reported by PUNCH; the commission's final register and any resulting disciplinary or criminal proceedings remain important next steps.

The concern is not limited to photographs. A credible register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Yiaga Africa's Samson Itodo and other civil-society representatives told Sunday PUNCH that the register is foundational to electoral credibility and called for an independent forensic audit with safeguards for personal data. The European Union Election Observation Mission had already identified weaknesses in Nigeria's register after the 2023 election, including deceased, emigrated and internally migrated voters and acknowledged under-age registrations.

The discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. One civil-society representative quoted by PUNCH explicitly warned against that conclusion without concrete evidence, while saying the irregularities could be exploited if left unresolved. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate and prosecute anyone found guilty. The commission should publish how the controls failed, the audit trail, the affected record categories and a clear process for eligible voters to challenge errors before the final register is released.

articles.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements; comments by Yiaga Africa and other civil-society representatives reported by PUNCH
articles.whyItMatters: A trustworthy register is the foundation of a credible election. Weak controls can undermine confidence before polling day, while careless clean-up can wrongly exclude eligible citizens.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, the final register, publication of audit findings, any prosecutions and accessible procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.

articles.title: Jonathan calls for end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy
articles.summary: Former President Goodluck Jonathan says money, patronage and ethnic considerations are weakening leadership selection and Nigeria's international reputation. He called for credible elections, internal party democracy and merit-based public appointments.
articles.content:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for reforms to Nigeria's political and leadership recruitment systems, arguing that money, patronage, ethnicity and personal connections too often outweigh competence and merit. Speaking at the Paul Alaje Colloquium in Abuja on Saturday, he said credible elections and stronger internal party democracy were essential to restoring the country's international standing.

Jonathan linked political practices to wider economic consequences, saying corruption, insecurity, abuse of public office and weak institutions undermine investor confidence and international partnerships. He also argued that Nigeria should invest more consistently in education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure, while supporting creative industries and sports as instruments of cultural diplomacy.

His remarks arrive as parties prepare for the 2027 general election and debate candidate selection, coalitions and electoral credibility. They are a former president's assessment and policy argument, not an independent measurement of every party's internal processes. The challenge for all political organisations is to demonstrate transparent primaries, fair access to party structures, credible candidate selection and accountability to members and voters.

articles.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
articles.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.
articles.content:
Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. Sunday PUNCH reports that the ADC and other opposition groups alleged that their campaign materials were being removed and that access to public facilities was being restricted.

In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

articles.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda

articles.content:
President Bola Tinubu used his visit to Ibadan on Saturday to seek South-West support for his administration and the APC's 2027 campaign. The Guardian reported that he told traditional rulers, led by the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, that the sacrifices associated with his economic reforms would lead to greater prosperity. Tinubu cited an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the former Leyland Automobile Assembly Plant, saying the project could support vehicle assembly and employment.

At the Mapo Hall rally, he endorsed APC candidates for Oyo, Ogun and Lagos and made a remark about a group he called the 'palẹmọ' faction. Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. RadiantWaves distinguishes the President's words from media interpretation.

The political test for the administration is whether the promised industrial activity, employment and economic reforms produce measurable benefits for households and businesses. The opposition is entitled to challenge the record, while the government should publish project milestones, financing details, job estimates and delivery dates.

articles.title: Akpabio urges parties to keep 2027 elections peaceful and reject do-or-die politics
articles.summary: Senate President Godswill Akpabio called on political actors to caution supporters and avoid tension, while reaffirming the administration's stated commitment to free, fair and credible elections.
articles.content:
Senate President Godswill Akpabio has urged politicians to prevent the 2027 general election from becoming a do-or-die contest. According to PUNCH, he made the remarks while receiving Ghana's Speaker of Parliament, Alban Bagbin, in Abuja. Akpabio said political actors should caution supporters against actions that could create tension and repeated the Federal Government's stated commitment to free, fair and credible elections.

Bagbin said Ghana was concerned about declining public confidence in democracy across the region and argued that political leaders must demonstrate that democratic government remains the best system. The exchange is significant because electoral violence and intimidation can undermine participation long before polling day.

The administration's assurance should be measured against practical safeguards: impartial policing, equal campaign access, protection of opposition candidates, credible voter registration, transparent results and prompt action against political violence. The same standards should apply to every party and every state.

articles.summary: President John Mahama has urged the parliamentary Minority to support a $10bn economic transformation programme for 2027–2030, arguing that its success should matter more than which party benefits politically.

Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama has urged the parliamentary Minority to support the government's proposed $10 billion New Economy programme, saying its success would benefit the country even if it helped keep the governing National Democratic Congress in power. The programme was outlined in Ghana's 2027 budget and is intended to support agriculture, energy infrastructure, critical minerals, tourism, textiles, pharmaceuticals and the technology economy. The Ghana News Agency reported that the government plans a US$10 billion investment framework between 2027 and 2030, with GH¢30 billion earmarked for the programme in 2027. The programme includes proposed investment in local food production, electricity generation and transmission, solar power, battery storage and value-added mineral processing.

The government's targets are ambitious and should be assessed against the final budget, financing sources, procurement transparency, implementation capacity and measurable jobs and productivity. Cross-party support does not remove the need for parliamentary scrutiny; it makes scrutiny and transparent reporting even more important.

articles.summary: Global InfoAnalytics data reported by Citi Newsroom says 51 per cent of young voters surveyed were satisfied with the 24-hour Economy policy, compared with 47 per cent of voters overall. The published summary does not provide full methodology.

A poll reported by Citi Newsroom on 21 November says 51 per cent of young voters expressed satisfaction with Ghana's 24-hour Economy policy, compared with 47 per cent of voters overall. The report says 32 per cent of young respondents were dissatisfied, compared with 34 per cent of voters overall. The policy is intended to encourage round-the-clock production, multiple work shifts, job creation and higher economic activity.

RadiantWaves therefore attributes the figures to Global InfoAnalytics as reported by Citi and does not present them as a definitive measure of all young Ghanaians.

For the policy to succeed, public approval will ultimately depend on whether businesses can operate safely and profitably across shifts, whether electricity and transport are reliable, and whether new jobs are decent and sustainable.

articles.title: France sees sixth weekend of protests over living costs, public services and student conditions
articles.summary: Reuters reports that turnout fell at largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday: the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 nationwide, while organisers estimated 150,000. Cost-of-living and student-rights concerns remain.
articles.content:
France experienced a sixth consecutive weekend of demonstrations on Saturday, 21 November, over the cost of living, student rights and public services. Reuters reported that the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 participants nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris. Organisers estimated 150,000 nationwide, including 45,000 in the capital. Both figures are attributed estimates and should not be combined. The previous Saturday's Interior Ministry count was 106,000, while organisers had estimated 200,000.

The movement began in September with students demanding renovated school buildings, more teachers and university reforms. It broadened into a wider campaign over purchasing power, public services and policing, drawing in trade unions and political activists. Reuters reported that about 70,000 security personnel were deployed and that most demonstrations were peaceful, although sporadic violence was reported, including in Marseille.

The lower turnout offers the government some respite, but does not establish that the underlying grievances have been resolved. Housing costs, wages, education resources and trust in policing remain politically sensitive as France approaches the 2027 presidential contest. The demonstrations should be assessed by their demands and the government's response, not simply by crowd size.

articles.title: Belgium warns of major flight cancellations during Monday's national strike
articles.summary: Air traffic controller Skeyes says it cannot guarantee regular air traffic from 7am to 9pm on Monday, 23 November. Brussels Airport expects most flights to be cancelled; essential emergency flights may continue.
articles.content:
Belgium is preparing for major disruption to air travel on Monday, 23 November, after air traffic controller Skeyes said staffing levels would not allow it to guarantee the safe handling of regular air traffic between 7am and 9pm. AFP reported that Brussels Airport expects the majority of arriving and departing flights to be cancelled. Charleroi Airport said the strike would shut down regular operations across the country's airports for the day.

The action is part of a national strike against government austerity measures and proposed savings intended to reduce Belgium's budget deficit. Skeyes said essential minimum services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would remain available. Passengers should check directly with their airline and airport before travelling, because schedules and cancellation policies may change.

The dispute reflects broader tensions over public spending, government cost-cutting and the effect of austerity on workers and essential services.

articles.title: UK and EU agree reset package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility
articles.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade / Youth
articles.summary: The 20 November Brussels summit produced a joint statement on closer food-trade, carbon-market and youth-opportunity cooperation. The UK government's projected £17bn annual economic benefit by 2040 is not a guaranteed outcome.
articles.content:
The United Kingdom and European Union agreed a new cooperation package at their summit in Brussels on 20 November. The European Council's joint statement confirms that Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The UK government says closer cooperation should reduce paperwork for food and drink exports, support manufacturers, link carbon-market arrangements and create new opportunities for young people to live, work, study and travel in Europe.

The government has presented the package as a pragmatic reset designed to reduce trade friction and support growth. It estimates that closer cooperation could add up to £17 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040; this is a government projection, not a guaranteed gain. The detailed eligibility rules, quotas and start dates for any youth-mobility scheme still require further legal and administrative work. The agreement does not mean the UK is rejoining the EU, the single market or the customs union.

The deal has already drawn domestic criticism. Sky News reported that Conservative politicians warned that linking emissions-trading schemes could raise household fuel costs, while university leaders expressed concern about the implications of tuition-fee parity for EU students. Those objections are political and sectoral assessments, not proof that the projected costs will occur. The next stage is to publish the legal texts, implementation timetable and independent impact assessments so households, businesses and universities can see who benefits and who may bear new costs.

articles.title: UK and Ukraine agree to manufacture longer-range drones on British soil
articles.category: Europe / United Kingdom / Ukraine / Defence / Industry
articles.summary: The UK Ministry of Defence says Ukrainian-designed strike drones will be manufactured in Britain for Ukraine's armed forces, adding industrial capacity to a wider £500m support package announced that week.
articles.content:
The United Kingdom and Ukraine have signed new agreements to enable Ukrainian-designed strike drones to be manufactured in Britain for Ukraine's armed forces, the UK Ministry of Defence said on 21 November. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara in Kyiv. The British government says the arrangement will add manufacturing capacity and strengthen supply chains for Ukraine as Russia's invasion continues.

The agreements follow a £500 million UK support package announced during the same week for drones, air-defence missiles, radars and other critical capabilities. The official statement does not provide production volumes, factory locations, delivery dates or the full technical specifications of the drones. Those details should not be inferred from the announcement.

The partnership is both a military-support measure and an industrial cooperation project. Its effectiveness will depend on production speed, supply-chain resilience, testing, training and the ability to deliver systems that meet Ukraine's operational requirements. It does not itself signal a ceasefire or a change in the battlefield situation.
