articles.title: Canada says military cooperation with US continues despite reported Pentagon restrictions
articles.category: North America / Canada / Defence / US Relations
articles.summary: Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty says he has seen no change in military cooperation with Washington despite a reported classified Pentagon memo. The memo has not been made public and its precise scope remains unclear.
articles.content:
Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said on 21 November that he had seen no change in military cooperation with the United States, despite a Washington Post report about a classified Pentagon directive imposing new restrictions on defence ties. Speaking to Reuters at a security conference in Halifax, McGuinty said the two militaries continued to work closely on continental defence, counter-narcotics operations, integrated missile systems and responses to threats in North American airspace.

The Washington Post report cited officials familiar with the memo but said it had not seen the document. Reuters reported that the Pentagon had not responded to its request for comment; a Pentagon spokesperson was quoted elsewhere as saying the guidance did not affect NATO, NORAD or intelligence operations. Republican Senator Mike Rounds said the memo contained no major measures beyond longstanding practice. The document's exact scope and practical effect therefore remain unclear.

McGuinty said Canada's 70-year NORAD relationship with the United States remained effective, while arguing that Canada must assume more responsibility for its own defence, particularly in the Arctic. Canada says it reached NATO's 2 per cent GDP spending target in 2025 and plans to increase defence spending to 5 per cent by 2035. The episode illustrates the tension between maintaining an integrated continental defence system and reducing strategic dependence on a neighbour whose political rhetoric has unsettled Canadian leaders.

articles.title: Factory fire in Indonesia leaves three dead and 36 workers unaccounted for
articles.summary: An AP report says three people died and 36 workers remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy factory in Banten. Fifteen people were rescued, including four injured; the cause has not been established.
articles.content:
A fire swept through the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Serang district, Banten province, on Saturday, 21 November. The Associated Press reported that three people had died and 36 workers remained unaccounted for as rescue teams searched the damaged facility. Fifteen people were rescued alive, including four injured workers. The factory produces Milkita milk-based sweets and snacks.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said search operations were continuing. More than 12 hours after the fire began, flames were still burning in parts of the facility, according to local rescue officials. Survivors suggested that the blaze may have started in a cooling unit on the third floor, but officials had not established the cause and had not confirmed whether all missing workers were inside when the fire began.

The immediate priority is locating missing workers and identifying the dead and injured. A later investigation will need to establish how the fire started, whether alarms and emergency exits were adequate, how quickly workers were evacuated and whether workplace fire-safety standards were followed. The incident adds to wider concerns about industrial safety and emergency preparedness.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns after AI-assisted exam cheating scandal
articles.category: Asia / South Korea / Education / Artificial Intelligence
articles.summary: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned and President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation after an AI-assisted exam-cheating scandal and criticism of last-minute security changes. Officials detected 111 electronic-device violations during the university entrance exam.
articles.content:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered his resignation on Sunday, 22 November, taking responsibility for confusion over anti-cheating measures before the country's high-stakes College Scholastic Ability Test, known as the Suneung. The presidential office said President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation. The controversy followed the confession of the top scorer in a national tax-accountant examination, who admitted using a miniature camera and smartphone to obtain a near-perfect score with the help of AI.

The government introduced emergency countermeasures before Thursday's university entrance examination, including restrictions on smart devices, inspections of clothing and accessories, and emergency alerts intended to identify phones that candidates had failed to surrender. The Guardian, citing official information, reported that 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were detected during the exam, nearly half through the emergency alerts. The minister said the government had not prepared adequately in advance and that last-minute changes inconvenienced students and the public.

The episode highlights a difficult balance: examination authorities must respond to increasingly sophisticated devices and AI tools without creating confusion, excessive surveillance or unfair treatment of candidates. The resignation is a political consequence; it does not resolve the wider challenge of protecting exam integrity in an era when images can be transmitted and analysed rapidly.

articles.title: Trump says he wants a permanent agreement preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon

articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said he intends to secure a permanent deal preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The statement describes his objective; it is not evidence that a new agreement has been negotiated or accepted by Tehran.

US President Donald Trump has said he intends to secure a permanent agreement with Iran that would prevent Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and bind future US administrations. Anadolu's Sunday morning briefing reported the remarks made on Saturday. Trump argued that the agreement should not be reversible by a future president.

The statement sets out the US President's desired outcome, but no completed agreement was announced in the report. Any durable nuclear arrangement would require negotiations over verification, sanctions, enrichment limits, monitoring, enforcement and the political commitments of both sides. Iran's position and response must be reported separately; a US declaration of intent does not amount to Iranian acceptance.

The issue carries implications for regional security, energy markets and diplomacy across the Gulf. A credible agreement would need clear verification mechanisms and a process for addressing disputes, rather than relying solely on political assurances.

articles.title: UNIFIL begins handing over some southern Lebanon positions to Lebanese army ahead of mandate end
articles.category: Middle East / Lebanon / United Nations / Security
articles.summary: UNIFIL's mission chief says some positions are being transferred to the Lebanese army as the force prepares for its mandate to end on 31 December 2026. The UN Security Council has authorised a phased drawdown and withdrawal during 2027.
articles.content:
UNIFIL has begun handing over some of its positions in southern Lebanon to the Lebanese army, mission chief Diodato Abagnara said on Saturday, according to Lebanon's National News Agency as reported by Anadolu. He warned against a security vacuum after the peacekeeping mission ends and said monitoring and reporting violations, humanitarian assistance and civilian protection remain important.

The UN Security Council's Resolution 2790 (2025) extended UNIFIL's mandate for a final time until 31 December 2026 and directed an orderly drawdown and withdrawal beginning at the end of the year, to be completed within one year. The resolution calls for stronger Lebanese army deployment and international support for its capabilities. UNIFIL has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978, with its mandate expanded after the 2006 conflict.

The handover is not simply an administrative transfer. Southern Lebanon remains affected by conflict and violations of the cessation-of-hostilities arrangement. The transition will depend on the Lebanese state's ability to provide security, the support available to its armed forces and whether a replacement international monitoring arrangement is agreed.

articles.title: COP31 negotiators present revised climate package as final approval remains unconfirmed
articles.summary: COP31 President Murat Kurum says a revised package could secure consensus on fossil-fuel language and adaptation finance. Delegates were due to begin considering approval on Sunday morning, but formal adoption was not confirmed in the sources reviewed by 07:28 CET.
articles.content:
Climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya continued beyond the summit's scheduled Friday finish and into Sunday, 22 November. Reuters reported that COP31 President Murat Kurum said a revised package had been presented which he believed all parties could accept. The conference was expected to reconvene on Sunday morning to begin approving the text after delegations had been given time to raise objections.

The revised package followed criticism of an earlier draft for omitting explicit reference to ending fossil-fuel use and for failing to provide a clear adaptation-finance pathway. Kurum said the new text addressed concerns about fossil fuels and financial support for developing countries adapting to climate change. Nearly 200 delegations are involved in the negotiations, with Australia leading the talks and Türkiye hosting the summit. The United States did not participate directly in the negotiations, according to AP.

A presidency statement that a text is acceptable is not the same as a formally adopted decision. At RadiantWaves' 07:28 CET verification point, the sources reviewed reported that an approval session was scheduled but did not confirm that the final cover decision had been adopted. The wording matters: climate-vulnerable countries are seeking predictable finance and stronger commitments, while economies dependent on fossil-fuel production and consumption resist language they consider too restrictive. The final document should be assessed against the actual adopted text, not the announcement of a compromise.

articles.title: AI-linked technology sell-off sends Nasdaq to its worst week since 2020
articles.category: Business / Global Markets / Artificial Intelligence / Technology
articles.summary: Reuters reports the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% on Friday and 10% over the week, while Nvidia dropped 14% in one session. Investors are reassessing valuations, financing and the pace of AI-related spending—not declaring the technology obsolete.
articles.content:
Technology shares suffered a sharp sell-off on Friday, 20 November. Reuters reported that the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% on the day and 10% over the week, its largest weekly decline since 2020. The S&P 500 fell 3.7%, while the VIX volatility index rose 33% to 37. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday and 23% for the week after Reuters reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was probing its accounting. Anthropic shares also fell after a high-profile initial public offering, and a semiconductor index of AI-linked companies recorded a broad retreat.

The market reaction reflects questions about how much future AI growth has already been priced into technology shares, the scale of data-centre investment, the availability and cost of financing, and whether expected earnings will justify current valuations. Reuters quoted investors who continued to believe in the long-term AI opportunity while acknowledging that higher interest rates and valuation expectations were creating a near-term test.

The fall does not prove that AI investment is ending or that the technology has failed. It shows that a transformative technology can attract capital and still carry substantial financial risk when company valuations assume rapid growth before the returns are established. The next evidence will come from company earnings, capital-spending plans, semiconductor demand and the cost of financing data-centre projects.

articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev are scheduled to contest the ATP Finals title in Turin on Sunday. Alcaraz reached the final after recovering to beat Ben Shelton; Zverev defeated Daniil Medvedev in straight sets.

The ATP Finals in Turin reach their conclusion on Sunday, with Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev scheduled to contest the title. The match is a test of consistency across the season's elite field rather than a standard knockout event. Alcaraz is seeking his first ATP Finals title after losing last year's final to Jannik Sinner. Zverev, a two-time champion, will rely on his serve and backhand in indoor conditions. articles.title: Zamfara bandits threaten to block 2027 voting as road control deepens
articles.summary: A SARI Global security report cited by Sunday PUNCH says armed leaders warned community representatives in Anka that elections would not be allowed. The report also describes road blockades, attacks, levies and displacement; its figures are not official government statistics.
articles.content:
Sunday PUNCH reported on 22 November that a SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026 described a threat by bandit leaders in Anka Local Government Area, Zamfara State, to prevent elections in their communities. The report says armed groups have tightened control over roads, burned vehicles, imposed a ₦50 million levy on communities in Dansadau District and displaced more than 300 residents.

According to SARI Global, Zamfara recorded 69 security incidents and 137 fatalities in October, making it the country's most incident-dense state in the firm's assessment. The report also says abduction cases nationwide rose to 55 in October from 27 in September. It describes attacks on roads, vehicles and escorted convoys, including an ambush in which at least 20 people were reportedly killed. These are figures and assessments from the private risk-intelligence report as reported by PUNCH, not a consolidated official national security dataset.

The alleged election threat is especially serious because it suggests armed groups may seek to control not only movement and commerce but also political participation. Zamfara has 14 local government areas and 3,529 polling units, according to INEC figures cited by PUNCH. If communities cannot travel safely, campaign, register or reach polling units, formal election dates alone will not guarantee equal participation.

Security agencies and INEC need to explain how they will protect roads, communities, election staff, observers and voters without placing civilians at greater risk. The government should publish credible incident data and the outcomes of operations, while avoiding claims that a threat has been neutralised before residents can safely resume normal movement.

articles.title: Nigeria opens bidding portal for 40 oil and gas blocks
articles.summary: The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission says registration opened on 20 November and closes on 15 January 2027. The offer includes 17 onshore, 14 shallow-water and nine deep-offshore blocks.
articles.content:
The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission has opened the portal for its 2026 oil and gas licensing round, offering 40 blocks to prospective investors. PUNCH reported on 22 November that registration began on Friday, 20 November, and will close on 15 January 2027. The blocks comprise 17 onshore, 14 shallow-water and nine deep-offshore assets.

The regulator says the process will run through five stages: registration and prequalification, access to data, submission of technical and commercial bids, technical evaluation and a commercial conference. A pre-bid conference is scheduled for Lagos on 16 December 2026. The commission says the portal provides the list of blocks, bidding guidance and frequently asked questions.

The licensing round is part of Nigeria's effort to attract capital, increase upstream production and improve competitiveness in the global energy market. However, a licensing round is not the same as immediate new production or revenue. Exploration, financing, environmental approvals, infrastructure, security and commercial development can take years. The credibility of the process will depend on transparent bid evaluation, clear contract terms, environmental safeguards, host-community engagement and public reporting of awards and obligations.

articles.title: Opposition coalition moves summit to 30 November and plans a one-day campaign pause
articles.summary: The Coalition for Democracy says ADC, APM, NDC, a PDP faction, PRP and SDP members will pause campaigns nationwide on 30 November to attend a summit. The meeting is intended to produce a common agreement, not yet a single presidential ticket.
articles.content:
The Coalition for Democracy has rescheduled its second summit from Monday, 23 November, to Monday, 30 November 2026, after member parties said campaign schedules could prevent presidential candidates, national chairmen and other leaders from attending. The committee's statement, signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman, says participating parties will pause campaign activities nationwide for the day so their representatives can attend.

The coalition emerged from the G100 Opposition Summit held in Abuja on 31 August. Its participating platforms include the African Democratic Congress, Allied Peoples Movement, Nigeria Democratic Congress, a faction of the Peoples Democratic Party, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party. Organisers say the 30 November meeting is intended to finalise and sign a common agreement ahead of the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

The move is evidence of coordination, but it is not proof that the parties have selected one presidential candidate or resolved their internal disputes. The coalition's credibility will depend on transparent decision-making, a clear policy programme, a fair process for any joint candidacy and respect for each party's constitutional procedures. Voters should be able to distinguish a temporary political agreement from a formal merger or a settled ticket.

articles.title: Separate court cases leave Atiku and the ADC facing two different legal tests
articles.summary: A 5 November Federal High Court judgment set aside the Mark-led ADC leadership process and Atiku Abubakar's nomination; the ADC said it would appeal. Separately, on 20 November, a judge refused to let Atiku and the ADC amend their Tinubu eligibility suit, leaving the original case pending.
articles.content:
Two separate legal proceedings are shaping the ADC's position ahead of Nigeria's 2027 election, and they must not be reported as one case. On 5 November, the Federal High Court in Abuja, presided over by Justice Peter Lifu, nullified the David Mark-led ADC leadership structure and set aside decisions taken under it, including the party process that produced Atiku Abubakar as its presidential candidate. The challenge was brought by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe, who argued that the leadership had not emerged through a valid national convention. Reuters reported that the ADC rejected the judgment as politically motivated and said it would appeal.

In a separate pre-election suit filed by Atiku and the ADC against President Bola Tinubu, the APC and INEC, Justice Inyang Ekwo on 20 November refused the plaintiffs permission to amend their case. The proposed amendments were rejected on procedural grounds because they would introduce new facts outside the constitutional 14-day period for pre-election matters. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. The case concerns allegations about an NYSC discharge certificate submitted in support of Tinubu's nomination; Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate. The ruling did not determine whether the certificate is genuine and did not dismiss the substantive suit.

The national ADC leadership judgment and the Tinubu eligibility case therefore have different parties, legal questions and procedural positions. PUNCH reported that INEC had received notice of the appeal against the 5 November judgment and would await the Court of Appeal's decision. The reports reviewed for this edition do not establish that the appeal has been finally decided or that the trial judgment has been set aside.

The public interest is the rule of law: court orders must be respected, appeals must be heard fairly, and political allegations must be tested through evidence. Neither the ADC's claim of political motivation nor the allegation about Tinubu's certificate should be presented as a judicial finding unless a court has actually made that finding.

articles.title: Trump order puts federal contractors at centre of coming congressional oversight battle
articles.summary: An executive order requires federal contractors to consult the White House and agencies before responding to certain congressional inquiries and to withhold material the administration considers privileged. Democrats call it an attack on oversight; the White House says it protects executive privilege.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump issued an executive order late on Friday requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with the administration before responding to certain inquiries from Congress. The Associated Press reported that companies must coordinate with the White House and relevant agencies on responses and withhold communications the administration considers protected by executive privilege. Contractors that do not comply could face termination of their contracts or suspension from future federal work.

The order applies to a large network of companies that do business with the federal government. It comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January and have signalled investigations into government contracts, including payments to companies linked to the President's family. The White House has also instructed agencies to seek approval before agreeing to congressional testimony.

Democratic lawmakers described the order as an attack on Congress's constitutional oversight authority and argued that contractors have a duty to provide truthful information when lawfully requested. The White House says it is protecting executive privilege from congressional overreach. Presidents of both parties have asserted executive privilege, but its scope is limited and disputes can lead to prolonged legal battles. Whether communications held by outside contractors qualify for the protection may be tested in court.

The central question is how to protect legitimate confidential executive deliberations without preventing Congress from investigating public spending, conflicts of interest or possible wrongdoing. The order does not settle that constitutional dispute; it creates a new point of conflict between the executive branch and the incoming Congress.

articles.source: Associated Press, 21 November 2026; White House executive order and fact sheet; statements by incoming House Oversight Committee Democrats

articles.title: German industrial union calls 23,000 workers out in Monday pay dispute
articles.summary: IG Metall says 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany will strike for 24 hours on Monday, 23 November. The union wants a 5% wage rise or firm commitments on investment, production sites and jobs.
articles.content:
Germany's powerful IG Metall union said on Sunday that it would escalate its industrial action with a 24-hour strike on Monday, 23 November, involving 23,000 workers across 19 companies in northern Germany. Reuters reported that the affected businesses include Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilder Meyer Werft and wind-energy company Siemens Gamesa. Around 12,300 employees had already taken part in strikes across 17 facilities on Friday, according to the union.

IG Metall is seeking a 5 per cent wage increase or, where companies want to depart from the industry-wide agreement, commitments on investment, products, site locations and employment. Employers have proposed no permanent pay increases for the first 20 months and a 1.3 per cent increase from July 2028. The dispute therefore concerns not only current pay but also the future of industrial production and secure jobs.

The walkout comes as German manufacturers face pressure from global competition, energy costs and the transition to electric vehicles and renewable-energy supply chains. The union's demands and employers' offer are competing negotiating positions; no settlement had been announced in the Reuters report. Disruption will depend on which plants and services are affected.

articles.title: Thousands march in Lisbon over wages, rent and rising living costs
articles.summary: Reuters reports that thousands marched in Lisbon on 21 November at the call of the CGTP union federation. The union wants higher wages and pensions, lower essential costs and action on housing affordability.
articles.content:
Thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Saturday, 21 November, despite heavy rain, to protest against rising living costs, low wages and a deepening housing crisis. Reuters reported that the demonstration was organised by CGTP, Portugal's largest trade union federation, which called for higher wages and pensions, lower prices for essential goods and services and measures to curb housing costs. The union described turnout as many thousands; police did not publish an estimate.

The economic pressure is visible in the figures cited by Reuters. Portugal's average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 per cent below the European Union average, according to Eurostat, while inflation reached 3.8 per cent in October, driven by food and energy prices. House prices have more than doubled since 2017 and rents for new leases have nearly doubled, intensifying pressure on younger people and households entering the housing market.

The demonstration follows weeks of housing activism in Lisbon and Porto and forms part of a wider European debate about purchasing power, public services and affordable housing. Protesters blamed government policy, while the government had not provided a response in the Reuters report. The figures show structural affordability pressure, but the march itself is not a national opinion poll.

articles.title: Gauteng coalition pact could sideline South Africa's DA in three major metros
articles.category: Africa / South Africa / Politics / Local Government
articles.summary: Mail & Guardian reports that the ANC and a broad group of parties have effectively concluded coalition negotiations for 10 of Gauteng's 11 municipalities, leaving the DA outside arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Final positions and governing modalities remain outstanding.
articles.content:
Coalition negotiations in South Africa's Gauteng province could reshape local political power and reverberate through the national government of unity. The Mail & Guardian reported on 20 November that the African National Congress and a broad group of parties had effectively concluded negotiations for coalition arrangements in 10 of Gauteng's 11 municipalities, with the Democratic Alliance excluded from arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. The parties still needed to allocate political positions and finalise governing modalities.

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba told the newspaper that negotiations with the ANC and other parties had effectively concluded. Under the proposed arrangement, Mashaba was set to become Johannesburg mayor, ActionSA's Nasiphi Moya would retain the Tshwane mayoralty and the ANC would nominate the mayor in Ekurhuleni. The coalition partners include the ANC, MK Party, EFF, ActionSA, Build One South Africa, Rise Mzansi, the SACP, IFP, ATM and Patriotic Alliance.

The DA was the largest single party in all three metros but did not win an outright majority. The Mail & Guardian reported that the ANC, EFF, ActionSA and MK Party together held a majority in each council. The DA warned that excluding it despite its position as the largest party would undermine the electoral outcome. ActionSA said its participation should be anchored in service delivery, financial stabilisation and infrastructure renewal.

The negotiations are not yet the same as a fully implemented coalition government. The allocation of portfolios, final agreements and performance commitments will determine whether the pact can deliver stable administration and better municipal services. The outcome could also affect the ANC–DA relationship in the national government of unity.

articles.title: Russian cargo ship burns in Baltic Sea after drone strike; 16 crew evacuated
articles.category: Europe / Russia / Finland / Ukraine War / Maritime Security
articles.summary: The Russian vessel Sparta II was struck by drones in international waters and drifted into Finnish waters. Finland said Ukraine was likely responsible, but the reason for the attack was unclear and Ukraine and Russia had not commented.
articles.content:
A Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, caught fire after being struck by two drones in international waters west of Russia's Gogland island on Saturday, 21 November, and later drifted into Finnish waters. Reuters reported that all 16 crew members evacuated into lifeboats and were transferred to another Russian vessel. Finnish authorities were leading the rescue effort while the fire continued.

Finland's armed forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack, but officials said the reason for targeting the ship was unclear. Ukraine and Russia had not commented in the reports reviewed. The vessel is owned by Oboronlogistika, a company that provides logistics services to Russia's Defence Ministry and is under US sanctions. Finnish officials said its cargo had not been confirmed, although it could include military materiel.

The incident has created a maritime and security challenge for Finland and other Baltic states. Finnish authorities imposed temporary aviation and maritime restrictions, and Sweden and Estonia assisted with security and rescue operations. Finnish officials also said a Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly entering Finnish airspace during the response. These details do not establish a deliberate attack on Finland or confirm the cargo carried by the ship.

The episode illustrates how the war in Ukraine can create risks beyond the battlefield, particularly when military-linked shipping, drones and rescue operations intersect near NATO territory.

articles.title: Bahrain reports Iranian strike on civilian industrial site as regional attacks intensify
articles.summary: Bahrain says an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility and started a fire without causing injuries. Its defence force says air defences intercepted further attacks; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to target US positions, a claim not independently confirmed by US Central Command.
articles.content:
Bahrain said on Saturday, 21 November, that an Iranian attack had struck a civilian industrial facility, causing a fire but no injuries, according to Reuters. Civil Defence teams were working to contain the blaze, but the Interior Ministry did not identify the site. Bahrain initially warned residents to move to a safe location, later issued an all-clear and then sent a second alert.

Bahrain's Defence Force said its air defences intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks and that falling shrapnel caused material damage but no casualties. Iran's Revolutionary Guards, in a statement carried by Iranian state media, said they had launched a combined missile-and-drone attack on US positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in retaliation for alleged US aggression and violations of Iranian airspace. US Central Command had not immediately responded to Reuters' request for comment.

The claims should remain distinct: Bahrain reported damage at an industrial facility and interceptions; Iran claimed to have attacked US positions; and the US had not publicly confirmed the Iranian account in the report reviewed. The incidents reflect wider regional escalation following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February and repeated attacks across Gulf states.

articles.title: Two tanker incidents reported near Oman's Khasab; responsibility remains unclear
articles.category: Middle East / Oman / Strait of Hormuz / Shipping / Energy
articles.summary: UKMTO reported two tankers struck by unidentified projectiles near Khasab on 21 November. No casualties were reported and the environmental impact was unknown; Iran's separate mine claim could not be linked independently to either incident.
articles.content:
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported two incidents involving tankers near Oman's Khasab on Saturday, 21 November. Reuters reported that one outbound vessel was struck on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab. A second tanker was reportedly hit in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of the port. It was not immediately clear whether the two reports concerned the same vessel.

UKMTO said no casualties had been reported and that the environmental impact remained unknown. Separately, Iran's navy said an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian account or establish whether it referred to either of the UKMTO incidents. RadiantWaves therefore does not describe the reported projectile strikes as confirmed Iranian mine attacks.

Khasab lies on Oman's Musandam Peninsula at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried nearly one-fifth of global crude-oil supplies before the conflict. Attacks or perceived risks can increase insurance costs, disrupt shipping schedules and affect energy prices even when crews escape without injury.

The priority is to establish the identity and condition of the vessels, determine whether any pollution occurred and clarify responsibility through evidence rather than competing claims.

articles.title: Fire at Iraq's Hartha power station kills four and injures 35
articles.category: Middle East / Iraq / Energy / Public Safety
articles.summary: Reuters reports that a fire involving a gas pipeline at the Hartha power station north of Basra killed at least four people and injured 35. The plant, with 800MW installed capacity, had been operating at about 400MW before the incident.
articles.content:
A fire at Iraq's Hartha power station north of Basra killed at least four people and injured 35 on Saturday, 21 November, Reuters reported, citing security officials. The blaze spread to neighbouring homes, where many casualties suffered burns or smoke inhalation. Civil Defence teams brought the fire under control, but operations at the power station were halted.

Iraq's Electricity Ministry said the incident involved a gas pipeline supplying the facility. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an urgent investigation to establish the cause and determine responsibility. The Hartha station has an installed generating capacity of 800 megawatts but had been operating at around 400 megawatts before the fire. Officials had not provided a full assessment of the damage at the time of the report.

The incident highlights the vulnerability of critical energy infrastructure in a country whose electricity system has struggled with underinvestment, maintenance problems and demand pressures. The fire's cause has not yet been established, so it would be premature to attribute it to negligence or sabotage. The investigation should examine pipeline integrity, maintenance records, emergency planning and the protection of nearby homes.

articles.title: China opposes US restriction on Chinese telecom firms' direct access to American phone numbers
articles.category: Asia / China / United States / Technology / Telecommunications
articles.summary: China's Commerce Ministry says it opposes the US FCC's vote to bar Chinese telecom companies from direct access to US phone numbers, citing national-security concerns. Beijing has warned of possible countermeasures.
articles.content:
China's Commerce Ministry said on Sunday, 22 November, that Beijing firmly opposes the US Federal Communications Commission's vote to bar Chinese telecommunications companies from directly accessing US phone numbers. Reuters reported that the FCC decision, announced on Thursday, cited national-security concerns and would affect China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers.

China's ministry urged Washington to withdraw the restrictions and said it would take necessary countermeasures if the ban proceeded. Beijing argued that the move would deepen separation between the two countries in telecommunications, communications, testing and certification, and said it ran counter to the consensus reached by their leaders. Those are the Chinese government's stated objections; the FCC's national-security rationale should be assessed from the regulator's own decision and supporting documents.

The dispute adds another layer to the US–China technology relationship, where telecom infrastructure, data security, access to numbering resources and supply-chain controls have become strategic issues. The reported restriction concerns direct access to US phone numbers, not a blanket prohibition on all Chinese telecommunications equipment or services in the United States.

articles.title: Myanmar's military-backed government accuses ASEAN of unfair treatment over summit exclusion
articles.category: Asia / Myanmar / ASEAN / Diplomacy / Human Rights
articles.summary: Myanmar's foreign ministry says ASEAN's refusal to grant full political representation is unfair. ASEAN leaders say representation could be restored gradually if the authorities make progress on the bloc's five-point peace consensus.
articles.content:
Myanmar's military-backed government criticised an ASEAN decision as unfair and imbalanced on Saturday, 21 November, accusing the regional grouping of discriminatory treatment because Myanmar is not granted full representation at its summits. Reuters reported that the foreign ministry said the decision issued at the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila failed to reflect what the authorities described as positive measures taken by the government.

ASEAN leaders said at the summit that full political representation could be restored gradually if Myanmar made progress on the bloc's five-point consensus, a framework intended to end the post-coup crisis. The Myanmar statement said there were no political prisoners and that more than 126,000 prisoners had received pardons or amnesties since the coup. The United Nations and human-rights organisations have reported thousands of political prisoners, so the government's claim is disputed and should not be presented as an established fact.

Myanmar has remained in turmoil since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021, triggering a civil war. Reuters cited UN estimates of about 100,000 deaths and more than 3.5 million people displaced. The ASEAN position reflects continued pressure for an end to violence and meaningful dialogue, while the authorities in Naypyidaw are seeking greater regional legitimacy.

The dispute is not simply about protocol at summits. It concerns whether regional engagement can encourage a political settlement, protect civilians and create conditions for a return to inclusive government.

articles.title: UK October borrowing comes in below forecasts, but record debt-interest costs remain
articles.category: Europe / United Kingdom / Economy / Public Finance
articles.summary: Reuters reports that the UK borrowed £17bn in October, below the £18bn forecast, and earlier borrowing was revised down by £3.6bn. The October debt-interest bill nevertheless reached a record £11.2bn.
articles.content:
Britain's government borrowed £17 billion in October, below the £18 billion median forecast in a Reuters poll, according to figures reported by Reuters on 20 November. The Office for National Statistics also revised borrowing from April to September down by £3.6 billion, largely because of stronger tax receipts and faster-than-expected third-quarter growth.

The current budget deficit for the year to October stood at £72.9 billion, more than 10 per cent lower than a year earlier and slightly below the Office for Budget Responsibility's March forecast. However, the public-finance picture remains difficult. The debt-interest bill reached £11.2 billion in October, the highest monthly figure for that month since records began and about a third higher than a year earlier. Spending in the first seven months of the financial year was £11.4 billion above forecast, including £5.7 billion more in debt interest.

The figures give Chancellor John Healey some limited relief but do not remove the pressure on the public finances. Higher inflation and interest rates can raise borrowing costs, while the government must balance public-service spending, investment and its fiscal rules. A single month below forecast should not be treated as proof that the budget challenge has been solved.

articles.title: Italian workers and students protest over wages, public services and spending priorities
articles.category: Europe / Italy / Labour / Education / Public Services
articles.summary: Reuters reports that tens of thousands joined a CGIL-led general strike on 20 November. The union says more than one million people took part in demonstrations across over 100 cities; the Interior Ministry said it was too early to publish its own estimate.
articles.content:
Tens of thousands of workers and students took to the streets across Italy on Friday, 20 November, as the CGIL trade union federation staged a general strike demanding higher wages and greater investment in public services. Reuters reported that the action involved private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare. Air and rail services were excluded from the general strike, while local transport operated under minimum-service requirements.

CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said more than one million people had participated in demonstrations across more than 100 cities. The Interior Ministry said it was too early to provide its own estimate. Those figures should therefore remain attributed to the union and not presented as an independently confirmed national count. The protests coincided with student demonstrations across Europe and reflected discontent over living costs, housing, education funding and military spending.

Italy's parliament is examining a proposed €26 billion budget for 2027. CGIL argues that the plan does not adequately support incomes and public services, while Industry Minister Adolfo Urso said he respected the right to demonstrate and expected the budget to be improved through parliamentary amendments. The strike illustrates the competing priorities facing the government: fiscal choices, wage recovery, public-service capacity and the cost of living.

articles.title: Verstappen wins Las Vegas Grand Prix as Norris and Piastri complete podium
articles.summary: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix for the third time in four years. Lando Norris finished second and Oscar Piastri third; George Russell hit the barriers with three laps remaining and finished ninth.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday night, 21 November, for the third time in four years, Reuters reported on Sunday. Lando Norris finished second and Oscar Piastri third after a 50-lap race with frequent changes of the lead. Mercedes rival George Russell hit the barriers with three laps remaining and finished ninth.

Reuters reported that Mercedes had already secured both championships and that 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli had become the youngest-ever Formula One world champion earlier in the month. Ferrari's race was also affected by a collision between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc; each received a separate 10-second penalty. The Las Vegas result is important to the remaining battle for the runner-up position and to the teams' end-of-season momentum.

articles.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: NEMA confirms 24 deaths as rescue operation continues
articles.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
articles.summary: Reuters reported on Sunday that NEMA confirmed 24 deaths and 24 survivors after Friday's boat disaster. This updates earlier public figures of 23 bodies recovered by Governor Douye Diri; authorities have not published a final passenger manifest or complete account of everyone aboard.
articles.content:
Reuters reported on 22 November that at least 24 people died when a crowded boat carrying mourners to a funeral in Bayelsa State capsized on Friday, 20 November. The National Emergency Management Agency said 24 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The report brings the national agency's figure into line with the 24 deaths cited by the Associated Press. It is a further update to the governor's earlier statement, carried by PUNCH late on Saturday, that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued.

The vessel was travelling from Ayama to Ukubie in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area for a burial ceremony. Police initially reported a mechanical fault. The governor said preliminary findings pointed to overloading, the absence of a passenger manifest and passengers not wearing life jackets. Police accounts reported by AP say passengers allegedly asked the operator to steer towards shore after the problem developed; the operator reportedly fled and the boat manager was taken into custody. These are investigative accounts, not findings of guilt.

The state government has announced an investigation and plans for a Maritime Task Force and modern boats. The central questions remain: how many people boarded, whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, whether life jackets were available, who was responsible for inspection and why safety rules were not enforced. A final casualty list and transparent findings are essential for affected families and public accountability.

articles.title: COP31 faces sharp criticism as final climate pact remains contested
articles.summary: Negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the scheduled close. A revised text was presented as a possible compromise, but the final package remained contested, with the EU and several countries objecting to weak fossil-fuel language and limited adaptation finance.
articles.content:
UN climate negotiations in Antalya, Türkiye, remained unresolved into Sunday, 22 November, after talks ran well beyond their scheduled Friday finish. Reuters reported that the COP31 presidency circulated a revised package and said it believed the text could win consensus. The proposal followed overnight consultations involving Türkiye, Australia and nearly 200 delegations.

The dispute centres on how explicitly the agreement should address the transition away from fossil fuels and how much predictable financial support should be provided to countries facing climate impacts. The Guardian's live reporting said the latest draft referred indirectly to the COP28 commitment on transitioning away from fossil fuels but did not explicitly name fossil fuels, and that a proposed $120 billion adaptation-finance target was absent. The European Union and several countries reportedly warned that the draft did not meet the scale of the climate challenge. The text could still be revised, adopted, rejected or left unresolved; no final adoption should be reported until the official UNFCCC decision is published.

The African Group of Negotiators separately expressed disappointment with aspects of the proposed outcomes on climate finance and Action for Climate Empowerment. Its chair questioned whether the process adequately reflected the positions of developing countries and said that implementation requires the means to implement. This is a substantive issue for African states: climate resilience requires predictable funding for adaptation, early-warning systems, agriculture, water, health infrastructure and energy access, not only declarations of ambition.

The test of the final outcome is therefore practical. Does it set credible expectations for finance? Does it give vulnerable countries a meaningful voice? Does it translate the energy transition into support for workers and communities? Until the adopted text is available, the summit's outcome must be described as contested rather than concluded.

articles.title: Gulf security fears deepen after tanker incidents and Bahrain industrial-site strike
articles.summary: Bahrain says an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility, while UKMTO reported two tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. Responsibility for the tanker incidents remains disputed; the US rejected Iran's separate claim that it damaged an American F-16.
articles.content:
Security concerns across the Gulf intensified on Sunday, 22 November, after Bahrain accused Iran of striking a civilian industrial facility, causing a fire and damage but no reported casualties. Bahrain's Interior Ministry said civil-defence teams responded. Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to have targeted US military positions and Patriot radar systems in Bahrain. Those claims should be attributed to Iran and not treated as independently verified.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that two tankers had been hit in the Strait of Hormuz. One was struck by an unidentified projectile and another suffered damage to its engine room, with no casualties reported at the time of the initial maritime alerts. Iran's army later said a ship had caught fire after entering a restricted area and striking a mine. The accounts have not established who was responsible for the incidents or whether they were connected.

Iran has also claimed that its air defences damaged a US F-16 over Gulf waters. US Central Command rejected that account and said all American fighter aircraft in the region were safe and accounted for. The difference between the claims is important: there is no independent confirmation of Iran's aircraft-damage assertion.

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and gas shipments. Continued threats can raise shipping insurance, freight and energy costs even when the physical flow of oil is not fully interrupted. Diplomatic contacts involving Qatar have continued, but public statements from Tehran and Washington show that major differences remain over sanctions, the blockade and Iran's nuclear programme.

articles.title: US share-market correction sharpens debate over AI valuations and investment risk
articles.summary: The S&P 500 has fallen 10% from its October high, entering correction territory, according to AP. Analysts disagree over whether this is a temporary repricing or a deeper warning about AI-related valuations, borrowing and profitability.
articles.content:
US equities have entered correction territory after the S&P 500 fell 10 per cent from its October high, the Associated Press reported on Sunday, 22 November. The decline has been driven by doubts about the valuations of artificial-intelligence companies, the scale of their borrowing and capital spending, the timing of returns, possible higher interest rates and regulatory pressure.

A correction is conventionally defined as a fall of at least 10 per cent from a recent peak. It does not automatically mean that a bear market or recession has begun. AP notes that corrections have occurred repeatedly during long bull markets and that their duration and eventual depth vary. Some analysts see the sell-off as a necessary reset after rapid gains; others warn that falling confidence could deepen if earnings fail to justify investment plans.

The AI economy is not one uniform trade. Chipmakers, data-centre operators, power suppliers and cloud providers face different demand, financing and pricing conditions. Strong demand for computing infrastructure does not guarantee that every company building it will earn an adequate return. Investors and businesses should distinguish reported orders and revenue from forecasts, and compare capital expenditure with cash generation rather than treating AI enthusiasm as proof of future profits.

For households, pension funds and businesses, the wider lesson is that technology transformation can be real while market prices remain vulnerable to over-optimism. A 10 per cent decline is a market threshold, not a verdict on the long-term value of artificial intelligence.

europeNews.title: France sees sixth weekend of protests over living costs, public services and student conditions
europeNews.summary: Reuters reports that turnout fell at largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday: the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 nationwide, while organisers estimated 150,000. Cost-of-living and student-rights concerns remain.
europeNews.content:
France experienced a sixth consecutive weekend of demonstrations on Saturday, 21 November, over the cost of living, student rights and public services. Reuters reported that the Interior Ministry counted 82,500 participants nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris. Organisers estimated 150,000 nationwide, including 45,000 in the capital. Both figures are attributed estimates and should not be combined. The previous Saturday's Interior Ministry count was 106,000, while organisers had estimated 200,000.

The movement began in September with students demanding renovated school buildings, more teachers and university reforms. It broadened into a wider campaign over purchasing power, public services and policing, drawing in trade unions and political activists. Reuters reported that about 70,000 security personnel were deployed and that most demonstrations were peaceful, although sporadic violence was reported, including in Marseille.

The lower turnout offers the government some respite, but does not establish that the underlying grievances have been resolved. Housing costs, wages, education resources and trust in policing remain politically sensitive as France approaches the 2027 presidential contest. The demonstrations should be assessed by their demands and the government's response, not simply by crowd size.

europeNews.title: UK and EU agree reset package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility
europeNews.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade / Youth
europeNews.summary: The 20 November Brussels summit produced a joint statement on closer food-trade, carbon-market and youth-opportunity cooperation. The UK government's projected £17bn annual economic benefit by 2040 is not a guaranteed outcome.
europeNews.content:
The United Kingdom and European Union agreed a new cooperation package at their summit in Brussels on 20 November. The European Council's joint statement confirms that Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The UK government says closer cooperation should reduce paperwork for food and drink exports, support manufacturers, link carbon-market arrangements and create new opportunities for young people to live, work, study and travel in Europe.

The government has presented the package as a pragmatic reset designed to reduce trade friction and support growth. It estimates that closer cooperation could add up to £17 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040; this is a government projection, not a guaranteed gain. The detailed eligibility rules, quotas and start dates for any youth-mobility scheme still require further legal and administrative work. The agreement does not mean the UK is rejoining the EU, the single market or the customs union.

The deal has already drawn domestic criticism. Sky News reported that Conservative politicians warned that linking emissions-trading schemes could raise household fuel costs, while university leaders expressed concern about the implications of tuition-fee parity for EU students. Those objections are political and sectoral assessments, not proof that the projected costs will occur. The next stage is to publish the legal texts, implementation timetable and independent impact assessments so households, businesses and universities can see who benefits and who may bear new costs.

europeNews.category: Europe / United Kingdom / Ukraine / Defence / Industry
europeNews.summary: The UK Ministry of Defence says Ukrainian-designed strike drones will be manufactured in Britain for Ukraine's armed forces, adding industrial capacity to a wider £500m support package announced that week.
europeNews.content:
The United Kingdom and Ukraine have signed new agreements to enable Ukrainian-designed strike drones to be manufactured in Britain for Ukraine's armed forces, the UK Ministry of Defence said on 21 November. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara in Kyiv. The British government says the arrangement will add manufacturing capacity and strengthen supply chains for Ukraine as Russia's invasion continues.

The agreements follow a £500 million UK support package announced during the same week for drones, air-defence missiles, radars and other critical capabilities. The official statement does not provide production volumes, factory locations, delivery dates or the full technical specifications of the drones. Those details should not be inferred from the announcement.

The partnership is both a military-support measure and an industrial cooperation project. Its effectiveness will depend on production speed, supply-chain resilience, testing, training and the ability to deliver systems that meet Ukraine's operational requirements. It does not itself signal a ceasefire or a change in the battlefield situation.

Employers have proposed no permanent pay increases for the first 20 months and a 1.3 per cent increase from July 2028. The dispute therefore concerns not only current pay but also the future of industrial production and secure jobs.

The walkout comes as German manufacturers face pressure from global competition, energy costs and the transition to electric vehicles and renewable-energy supply chains. The union's demands and employers' offer are competing negotiating positions; no settlement had been announced in the Reuters report. Disruption will depend on which plants and services are affected.

europeNews.title: Thousands march in Lisbon over wages, rent and rising living costs
europeNews.summary: Reuters reports that thousands marched in Lisbon on 21 November at the call of the CGTP union federation. The union wants higher wages and pensions, lower essential costs and action on housing affordability.
europeNews.content:
Thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Saturday, 21 November, despite heavy rain, to protest against rising living costs, low wages and a deepening housing crisis. Reuters reported that the demonstration was organised by CGTP, Portugal's largest trade union federation, which called for higher wages and pensions, lower prices for essential goods and services and measures to curb housing costs. The union described turnout as many thousands; police did not publish an estimate.

The economic pressure is visible in the figures cited by Reuters. Portugal's average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 per cent below the European Union average, according to Eurostat, while inflation reached 3.8 per cent in October, driven by food and energy prices. House prices have more than doubled since 2017 and rents for new leases have nearly doubled, intensifying pressure on younger people and households entering the housing market.

The demonstration follows weeks of housing activism in Lisbon and Porto and forms part of a wider European debate about purchasing power, public services and affordable housing. Protesters blamed government policy, while the government had not provided a response in the Reuters report. The figures show structural affordability pressure, but the march itself is not a national opinion poll.

Air and rail services were excluded from the general strike, while local transport operated under minimum-service requirements.

Italy's parliament is examining a proposed €26 billion budget for 2027. CGIL argues that the plan does not adequately support incomes and public services, while Industry Minister Adolfo Urso said he respected the right to demonstrate and expected the budget to be improved through parliamentary amendments. The strike illustrates the competing priorities facing the government: fiscal choices, wage recovery, public-service capacity and the cost of living.

europeNews.title: UK October borrowing comes in below forecasts, but record debt-interest costs remain
europeNews.category: Europe / United Kingdom / Economy / Public Finance
europeNews.summary: Reuters reports that the UK borrowed £17bn in October, below the £18bn forecast, and earlier borrowing was revised down by £3.6bn. The October debt-interest bill nevertheless reached a record £11.2bn.
europeNews.content:
Britain's government borrowed £17 billion in October, below the £18 billion median forecast in a Reuters poll, according to figures reported by Reuters on 20 November. The Office for National Statistics also revised borrowing from April to September down by £3.6 billion, largely because of stronger tax receipts and faster-than-expected third-quarter growth.

The current budget deficit for the year to October stood at £72.9 billion, more than 10 per cent lower than a year earlier and slightly below the Office for Budget Responsibility's March forecast. However, the public-finance picture remains difficult. The debt-interest bill reached £11.2 billion in October, the highest monthly figure for that month since records began and about a third higher than a year earlier. Spending in the first seven months of the financial year was £11.4 billion above forecast, including £5.7 billion more in debt interest.

The figures give Chancellor John Healey some limited relief but do not remove the pressure on the public finances. Higher inflation and interest rates can raise borrowing costs, while the government must balance public-service spending, investment and its fiscal rules. A single month below forecast should not be treated as proof that the budget challenge has been solved.

For the policy to succeed, public approval will ultimately depend on whether businesses can operate safely and profitably across shifts, whether electricity and transport are reliable, and whether new jobs are decent and sustainable.

africaNews.title: Gauteng coalition pact could sideline South Africa's DA in three major metros
africaNews.category: Africa / South Africa / Politics / Local Government
africaNews.summary: Mail & Guardian reports that the ANC and a broad group of parties have effectively concluded coalition negotiations for 10 of Gauteng's 11 municipalities, leaving the DA outside arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Final positions and governing modalities remain outstanding.
africaNews.content:
Coalition negotiations in South Africa's Gauteng province could reshape local political power and reverberate through the national government of unity. The Mail & Guardian reported on 20 November that the African National Congress and a broad group of parties had effectively concluded negotiations for coalition arrangements in 10 of Gauteng's 11 municipalities, with the Democratic Alliance excluded from arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. The parties still needed to allocate political positions and finalise governing modalities.

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba told the newspaper that negotiations with the ANC and other parties had effectively concluded. Under the proposed arrangement, Mashaba was set to become Johannesburg mayor, ActionSA's Nasiphi Moya would retain the Tshwane mayoralty and the ANC would nominate the mayor in Ekurhuleni. The coalition partners include the ANC, MK Party, EFF, ActionSA, Build One South Africa, Rise Mzansi, the SACP, IFP, ATM and Patriotic Alliance.

The DA was the largest single party in all three metros but did not win an outright majority. The Mail & Guardian reported that the ANC, EFF, ActionSA and MK Party together held a majority in each council. The DA warned that excluding it despite its position as the largest party would undermine the electoral outcome. ActionSA said its participation should be anchored in service delivery, financial stabilisation and infrastructure renewal.

The negotiations are not yet the same as a fully implemented coalition government. The allocation of portfolios, final agreements and performance commitments will determine whether the pact can deliver stable administration and better municipal services. The outcome could also affect the ANC–DA relationship in the national government of unity.

africaNews.title: COP31 faces sharp criticism as final climate pact remains contested
africaNews.summary: Negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the scheduled close. A revised text was presented as a possible compromise, but the final package remained contested, with the EU and several countries objecting to weak fossil-fuel language and limited adaptation finance.
africaNews.content:
UN climate negotiations in Antalya, Türkiye, remained unresolved into Sunday, 22 November, after talks ran well beyond their scheduled Friday finish. Reuters reported that the COP31 presidency circulated a revised package and said it believed the text could win consensus. The proposal followed overnight consultations involving Türkiye, Australia and nearly 200 delegations.

The dispute centres on how explicitly the agreement should address the transition away from fossil fuels and how much predictable financial support should be provided to countries facing climate impacts. The Guardian's live reporting said the latest draft referred indirectly to the COP28 commitment on transitioning away from fossil fuels but did not explicitly name fossil fuels, and that a proposed $120 billion adaptation-finance target was absent. The European Union and several countries reportedly warned that the draft did not meet the scale of the climate challenge. The text could still be revised, adopted, rejected or left unresolved; no final adoption should be reported until the official UNFCCC decision is published.

The African Group of Negotiators separately expressed disappointment with aspects of the proposed outcomes on climate finance and Action for Climate Empowerment. Its chair questioned whether the process adequately reflected the positions of developing countries and said that implementation requires the means to implement. This is a substantive issue for African states: climate resilience requires predictable funding for adaptation, early-warning systems, agriculture, water, health infrastructure and energy access, not only declarations of ambition.

The test of the final outcome is therefore practical. Does it set credible expectations for finance? Does it give vulnerable countries a meaningful voice? Does it translate the energy transition into support for workers and communities? Until the adopted text is available, the summit's outcome must be described as contested rather than concluded.

nigeriaNews.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: death toll rises as governor orders investigation and safety enforcement
nigeriaNews.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
nigeriaNews.summary: Governor Douye Diri says 23 bodies have been recovered and 24 survivors rescued; AP, citing NEMA, reports 24 deaths. The discrepancy remains unresolved as authorities investigate overloading, missing passenger records and the absence of life jackets.
nigeriaNews.content:
A boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. Preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets.

The casualty figures are not yet consistent across reports. PUNCH carried the governor's update of 23 recovered bodies and 24 survivors. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reported at least 24 deaths and 24 rescues. The earlier police account had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving reports from separate briefings; RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than presenting one figure as final. Police said the boat reportedly developed a mechanical fault, that passengers urged the operator to head for the riverbank, and that the operator allegedly continued before the vessel capsized. The operator reportedly fled, while the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. Those claims require investigation and do not establish criminal guilt.

President Bola Tinubu expressed condolences and directed federal disaster-response agencies to support recovery and rescue work. PUNCH reported that he observed a minute of silence at the Ibadan APC rally and said Vice-President Kashim Shettima would visit Bayelsa. The governor has also announced plans for modern boats and a Maritime Task Force. Those proposals must be matched by transparent budgets, inspection schedules, passenger manifests, enforceable capacity limits, compulsory life jackets, trained operators and reliable rescue capacity.

The investigation should establish how many people were on board, whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and which agencies were responsible for enforcement. Replacing unsafe boats alone will not solve a system in which overloading and weak inspections can become normal practice. Families need an accurate casualty list, a transparent investigation and practical safeguards before the next journey.

nigeriaNews.title: Zamfara bandits threaten to block 2027 voting as road control deepens
nigeriaNews.summary: A SARI Global security report cited by Sunday PUNCH says armed leaders warned community representatives in Anka that elections would not be allowed. The report also describes road blockades, attacks, levies and displacement; its figures are not official government statistics.
nigeriaNews.content:
Sunday PUNCH reported on 22 November that a SARI Global Nigeria Monthly Security Overview for October 2026 described a threat by bandit leaders in Anka Local Government Area, Zamfara State, to prevent elections in their communities. The report says armed groups have tightened control over roads, burned vehicles, imposed a ₦50 million levy on communities in Dansadau District and displaced more than 300 residents.

According to SARI Global, Zamfara recorded 69 security incidents and 137 fatalities in October, making it the country's most incident-dense state in the firm's assessment. The report also says abduction cases nationwide rose to 55 in October from 27 in September. It describes attacks on roads, vehicles and escorted convoys, including an ambush in which at least 20 people were reportedly killed. These are figures and assessments from the private risk-intelligence report as reported by PUNCH, not a consolidated official national security dataset.

The alleged election threat is especially serious because it suggests armed groups may seek to control not only movement and commerce but also political participation. Zamfara has 14 local government areas and 3,529 polling units, according to INEC figures cited by PUNCH. If communities cannot travel safely, campaign, register or reach polling units, formal election dates alone will not guarantee equal participation.

Security agencies and INEC need to explain how they will protect roads, communities, election staff, observers and voters without placing civilians at greater risk. The government should publish credible incident data and the outcomes of operations, while avoiding claims that a threat has been neutralised before residents can safely resume normal movement.

nigeriaNews.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
nigeriaNews.summary: Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records entered the preliminary register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid records, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states; the findings do not prove a coordinated rigging plot.
nigeriaNews.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says questionable records were flagged during the nationwide display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and that INEC later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, told the newspaper that some registration officers had used their official login details to introduce questionable records but could not explain their actions.

INEC's wider clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 records: 1,608,660 confirmed invalid registrations and 873 records belonging to verified deceased people. The commission also identified 54 people across 10 states as implicated in registration irregularities. The figures are attributed to INEC statements reported by PUNCH; the commission's final register and any resulting disciplinary or criminal proceedings remain important next steps.

The concern is not limited to photographs. A credible register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Yiaga Africa's Samson Itodo and other civil-society representatives told Sunday PUNCH that the register is foundational to electoral credibility and called for an independent forensic audit with safeguards for personal data. The European Union Election Observation Mission had already identified weaknesses in Nigeria's register after the 2023 election, including deceased, emigrated and internally migrated voters and acknowledged under-age registrations.

The discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. One civil-society representative quoted by PUNCH explicitly warned against that conclusion without concrete evidence, while saying the irregularities could be exploited if left unresolved. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate and prosecute anyone found guilty. The commission should publish how the controls failed, the audit trail, the affected record categories and a clear process for eligible voters to challenge errors before the final register is released.

nigeriaNews.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements; comments by Yiaga Africa and other civil-society representatives reported by PUNCH
nigeriaNews.whyItMatters: A trustworthy register is the foundation of a credible election. Weak controls can undermine confidence before polling day, while careless clean-up can wrongly exclude eligible citizens.
nigeriaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, the final register, publication of audit findings, any prosecutions and accessible procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.

nigeriaNews.title: Jonathan calls for end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy
nigeriaNews.summary: Former President Goodluck Jonathan says money, patronage and ethnic considerations are weakening leadership selection and Nigeria's international reputation. He called for credible elections, internal party democracy and merit-based public appointments.
nigeriaNews.content:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for reforms to Nigeria's political and leadership recruitment systems, arguing that money, patronage, ethnicity and personal connections too often outweigh competence and merit. Speaking at the Paul Alaje Colloquium in Abuja on Saturday, he said credible elections and stronger internal party democracy were essential to restoring the country's international standing.

Jonathan linked political practices to wider economic consequences, saying corruption, insecurity, abuse of public office and weak institutions undermine investor confidence and international partnerships. He also argued that Nigeria should invest more consistently in education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure, while supporting creative industries and sports as instruments of cultural diplomacy.

His remarks arrive as parties prepare for the 2027 general election and debate candidate selection, coalitions and electoral credibility. They are a former president's assessment and policy argument, not an independent measurement of every party's internal processes. The challenge for all political organisations is to demonstrate transparent primaries, fair access to party structures, credible candidate selection and accountability to members and voters.

nigeriaNews.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
nigeriaNews.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.

Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

nigeriaNews.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda

Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. The political test for the administration is whether the promised industrial activity, employment and economic reforms produce measurable benefits for households and businesses. The opposition is entitled to challenge the record, while the government should publish project milestones, financing details, job estimates and delivery dates.
